description: Historical world-state timeline 1337–1837, compiled 2026-10-21. Covers territory (ownership_region, ownership), formations, capital moves, state religion changes, foreign merchant residencies, royal marriages, and diplomacy. All facts are commodity-neutral (goods='all'). Groups: af=111, dip=25, eu=127, mar=266, me=258, ru=53, rw=39, sa=564. Compiled under rules in docs/design/obsession/24_Historical_World_Timeline.md. East Asia (ea_) and residency follow-ups (re_) not yet complete: see 24 §5 gaps.
known_gaps: ea_ (East Asia) not compiled — API timeout during parallel compilation; use existing CHI/JAP/KOR 1337 tags only for now
re_ (Indian Ocean / East residencies) not compiled — API timeout; foreign merchant contacts in Asian markets absent
dip_: missing Safavid/Mughal/Muscovy resident missions, Moroccan, Crimean, various bilateral residencies
ru_: missing Nogai Horde, Khanate of Sibir, Kazakh steppe, Russian America, Caucasian annexations 1804-28
mar_: duplicate flags for Mary QoS/Francis II and Mary I/Philip II need deduplication
af_: Kanem Bulala period, Canaries (most islands), Congo civil war details absent

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 24 'The Horn of Africa'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi ('Gran') overruns the central Ethiopian highlands between 1531 and 1535 and holds them for nearly a decade until his death at Wayna Daga in 1543.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Asante conquers the old Akan kingdom of Bono-Takyiman to the north-west in the early 1720s, absorbing its gold and kola trade.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Kumasi and its immediate districts, the metropolitan province of Asante.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Osei Tutu and the Golden Stool confederacy defeat Denkyira in 1700-1 and build the Asante union with its capital at Kumasi.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 17 'Kanem-Borno: its relations with the Mediterranean Sea, Bagirmi and other states in the Chad basin'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Bagirmi's core territory on the Chari, a tributary zone contested with Borno and Wadai.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 17 'Kanem-Borno: its relations with the Mediterranean Sea, Bagirmi and other states in the Chad basin'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The sultanate of Bagirmi forms south-east of Lake Chad in the first half of the sixteenth century, with its capital at Massenya; it is repeatedly contested between Borno and Wadai.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 6 'The impact of the Mfecane on the Cape Colony'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: The Cape returns to the Batavian Republic in 1803 under the Peace of Amiens, and is again taken by Britain in 1806.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 17 'Kanem-Borno: its relations with the Mediterranean Sea, Bagirmi and other states in the Chad basin'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Mai Ali Gaji ends the Bulala wars and fixes the Sayfawa capital at Ngazargamu in Bornu, west of Lake Chad, around 1470.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 2 'African political, economic and social structures during this period'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Castile completes the conquest of La Palma by 1495, the island being the second-to-last of the Canaries to be subdued.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 2 'African political, economic and social structures during this period'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Castile takes Tenerife in 1495, completing the conquest of the Canary Islands; La Laguna (Aguere) becomes the island's administrative centre.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 15 'Fon and Yoruba: the Niger delta and the Cameroon'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Dahomean heartland around Abomey on the Abomey plateau.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 15 'Fon and Yoruba: the Niger delta and the Cameroon'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: King Agaja conquers Allada (Ardra), the older Aja kingdom of the coastal plain, in 1724.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 15 'Fon and Yoruba: the Niger delta and the Cameroon'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Fon migrants from Allada settle at Abomey around 1625 and build the kingdom of Dahomey, out of reach of the coastal slave ports.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 15 'Fon and Yoruba: the Niger delta and the Cameroon'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Dahomey conquers Whydah (Glexwe) in 1727, taking direct control of the coast's principal slave port.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 7 'The Sudan, 1500-1800'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Darfur and the Kordofan approaches pass from the Daju and the Nubian kings to the Keira sultans.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 7 'The Sudan, 1500-1800'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Sulayman Solongdungu founds the Kayra (Keira) dynasty of Darfur around 1640, with its capital at Uri; Islam becomes the court religion under his successors.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 11 'The end of the Songhay empire'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: After the Moroccan conquest the Askiya dynasty survives as a rump state in Dendi, downriver from Gao, with its capital at Lulami (map: Kukiya); it keeps a precarious unity until mid-century, signing a treaty with the Moroccans in 1630 and suffering pasha interventions in the 1630s.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Dutch take Arguin in the 1630s and keep a fort in the growing gum trade on the Mauritanian coast until the French recover it in 1723-24.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 23 'Southern Africa'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Jan van Riebeeck founds the Dutch refreshment station at Table Bay in 1652; the Company's cultivated district on the Cape peninsula is the first permanently held European territory in southern Africa.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 23 'Southern Africa'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Free burghers and trekboers spread the Dutch colony inland from Stellenbosch (1679) and Drakenstein to Swellendam and the eastern frontier districts during the eighteenth century, taking the Cape peninsula's hinterland from the Khoikhoi chiefdoms.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 1 'The struggle for international trade and its implications for Africa' (Dutch masters of Goree 1621, El Mina 1637, Arguin 1638); https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Dutch take Elmina castle in 1637 and hold it with a resident garrison and traders until the end of the period; the town and its Akan hinterland remain under African rulers.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Dutch occupy Goree from 1621 and use it as their Senegambian base; the sources disagree on the precise order of Dutch, Portuguese and English seizures before the French take the island in 1677.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Dutch occupy Mauritius from 1638, using it for ebony and as a refreshment stop; they abandon the island in 1710.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: English traders maintain a fortified factory on Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone estuary, the main British slave-trading station of the Windward Coast, until the abolition of the trade.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 23 'Southern Africa'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: A British squadron seizes Cape Town in 1795 during the French revolutionary wars; Britain holds the colony until the Peace of Amiens.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 6 'The impact of the Mfecane on the Cape Colony'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Britain occupies the Cape permanently from 1806 (ceded in 1814); the colony expands eastward to the Fish River and beyond during the period.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: An English chartered company holds Cape Coast Castle (map: Cabo Corso) from 1664, with a resident factor and garrison; Cape Coast grows into an independent coastal town, breaking away from the inland state of Fetu.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Britain occupies Goree during the Napoleonic wars; France reoccupies the island in 1817.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The English build Fort St James at the mouth of the Gambia in 1651 (map: Juffure); it controls the river trade and is held with interruptions until the French destroy it in 1779.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: A British expedition takes Mauritius in 1810; the island is ceded to Britain in 1814 and remains a British colony.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: The Sierra Leone colony founded in 1787, with Freetown from 1792 and Crown Colony status from 1808, gives Britain a territorial foothold in the Temne country of Upper Guinea, used as the base of the anti-slavery patrol.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The British occupy Saint-Louis from 1758 during the Seven Years' War and hold it until the French recover it in 1779.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Saint-Louis falls into British hands between 1809 and 1817.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 24 'The Horn of Africa'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Fasiladas makes Gondar a fixed imperial residence in 1636, ending the tradition of itinerant royal camps; Gondar remains the capital of Christian Ethiopia until 1855.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: A French expedition from Saint-Louis recovers the fort of Arguin from the Dutch in 1723-24; the Mauritanian coast post stays in French hands thereafter.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The French take Goree from the Dutch in 1677 and hold the island as their Senegambian trading base until the British occupation of 1800.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: France reoccupies Goree in 1817 and keeps it to the end of the period as the naval station for the anti-slave-trade patrol.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: France claims Mauritius in 1715 and colonizes it from Reunion by 1721 as the Ile de France, the naval base of the French East India Company.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Reunion (Bourbon) receives its first French settlers from Fort Dauphin in 1646 and 1654, and is made a French East India Company preserve from 1664.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Island of Saint-Louis'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/956/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Saint-Louis at the mouth of the Senegal is founded in 1659 as the first French chartered company post on the Atlantic coast of Africa.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: France recovers Saint-Louis in 1779 and holds it until the British occupation of 1809.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: France reoccupies Saint-Louis in 1817 and keeps it as the capital of its Senegalese colony to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 7 'The Sudan, 1500-1800'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Gezira and Butana between the Blue and White Nile, the core of the Funj sultanate, taken from the Alwa kings and the Arab riverain lords.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 7 'The Sudan, 1500-1800'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Funj sultanate is founded with its centre at Sennar in 1504, absorbing the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alwa.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 24 'States and peoples of Senegambia and Upper Guinea'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: The Futa Jallon plateau, core territory of the imamate after the jihad of the 1720s.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Fulbe Muslim revolution of Karamokho Sambegu establishes the imamate of Futa Jallon in the highlands of Guinea, with its capital at Timbo.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Sulayman Baal leads the Torodbe revolution in Futa Toro in 1775-76, replacing the Denianke kings with an elected almami and an Islamic state on the middle Senegal.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Futa Toro riverain provinces of Galam and Takrur, the seat of the Torodbe imamate.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 12 'From the Niger to the Volta'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Kaarta's core territory around Nioro, taken from the Soninke and Diarra polities of the region.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 12 'From the Niger to the Volta'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Bamana kingdom of Kaarta emerges west of Segou in the mid-eighteenth century, with its capital at Nioro.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Kwango valley heartland of Kasanje, on the slave route between the Lunda country and the Portuguese ports.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Imbangala leader Kasanje founds a base in the Kwango valley in 1626 and builds the Imbangala kingdom of Kasanje during the 1630s; it becomes the main entrepot for slaves moving from the interior to Luanda.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 16 'The Hausa states'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Kebbi's core territory on the Kebbi river, held against Songhay, Borno and the Hausa neighbours.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 16 'The Hausa states'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Kanta Kotal breaks Kebbi away from Songhay around 1516 and rules from Surame; Kebbi remains an independent Hausa kingdom until the Sokoto jihad.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 22 'Equatorial Africa and Angola: migrations and the emergence of the first states'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Afonso I makes Christianity the court religion of Kongo after 1506; the kingdom keeps a Catholic monarchy and a bishopric at Mbanza Kongo (Sao Salvador) through the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 22 'Equatorial Africa and Angola: migrations and the emergence of the first states'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: The Loango coast and its hinterland, the core of the kingdom.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 22 'Equatorial Africa and Angola: migrations and the emergence of the first states'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Loango, north of Kongo on the Atlantic coast, is one of the two great kingdoms the Portuguese found on that coast; it is already established in the fifteenth century and survives as a decentralised state to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 20 'The political system of the Luba and Lunda: its emergence and expansion'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Lunda heartland around the mussumba on the upper Lualaba.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 20 'The political system of the Luba and Lunda: its emergence and expansion'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Lunda empire takes shape under the Mwant Yav title around 1600, with its capital (mussumba) in the Lualaba country; it expands west and south through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

facts.source: Y. Person, 'Nyaani Mansa Mamudu et la fin de l'empire du Mali', Publications de la Societe francaise d'histoire des outre-mers (1981), pp. 613-653; https://www.persee.fr/doc/sfhom_1768-7144_1981_mel_5_2_965 ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV (1984), ch. 7 'The decline of the Mali empire'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: The Bamana kingdoms take over Mali's remaining heartland around Niani and the upper Niger in the later seventeenth century, ending the Mali empire as a territorial power.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 23 'Massina and the Torodbe (Tukuloor) empire until 1878'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Massina takes Djenne in 1818-19, the commercial centre of the middle Niger.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 23 'Massina and the Torodbe (Tukuloor) empire until 1878'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Seku Amadu founds the Fulbe caliphate of Massina after the jihad of 1818, with its capital at Hamdullahi in the inland Niger delta.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 23 'Massina and the Torodbe (Tukuloor) empire until 1878'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Massina's home territory in the inland Niger delta, the base of the 1818 jihad.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 23 'Massina and the Torodbe (Tukuloor) empire until 1878'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Massina takes Timbuktu from the Arma in 1825-26, ending the pashalik of Timbuktu.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 16 'Madagascar 1800-80'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Radama I conquers the Sakalava kingdom of Boina on the north-west coast in 1823-24, taking its port at Mahajanga (Majunga).

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Antananarivo and the Merina heartland, the base of Andrianampoinimerina's unification of Imerina.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 28 'Madagascar and the islands of the Indian Ocean'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Andrianampoinimerina, ruler of Ambohimanga from c.1785, reunifies central Imerina; he takes Antananarivo in the 1790s (1791-92 or 1797 depending on the chronicle) and makes it the capital of a single Merina kingdom.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 16 'Madagascar 1800-80'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Radama I extends Merina power east to the Betsimisaraka coast and the port of Toamasina (Tamatave) after the 1817 treaty with Britain.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 22 'Southern Zambezia'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Mutapa core in the Mazoe valley (Zvongombe and the Dande), which the dynasty retains after losing the plateau in the eighteenth century.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 21 'The Zambezi and Limpopo basins: 1100-1500'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 22 'Southern Zambezia'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The first Mwene Mutapa, Mutota, and his son Mutope extend the Zimbabwe culture's political system north into the Mazoe valley; the state's capital moves north from Great Zimbabwe.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Ndongo's core territory in the Kwanza valley, contested with Portugal through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The kingdom of Ndongo, whose ruler bore the title ngola (the origin of 'Angola'), takes shape south of Kongo around 1500; it is destroyed by the Portuguese in 1671.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Omani Arabs take Kilwa in 1784 and Zanzibar in 1785, and claim sovereignty over the Swahili towns on that coast.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Omani forces take Fort Jesus in 1698, ending Portuguese control of the East African coast north of Cape Delgado; Mombasa is afterwards ruled by Omani governors, from the 1740s the Mazrui family.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Zanzibar passes under Omani rule in 1785 and becomes the Busaidi dynasty's main stronghold on the coast.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 11 'The end of the Songhay empire'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: After the battle of Tondibi (March 1591) the Moroccan expeditionary force under Judar Pasha installs itself at Timbuktu as a pashalik; the Arma descend from these soldiers and rule the Niger bend until the Massina conquest.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 11 'The end of the Songhay empire'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The pashalik of Timbuktu governs Timbuktu and the middle Niger towns taken from Songhay (Djenne remained outside Arma control); pashas were appointed from Marrakesh in the first decades and the Arma chose them locally from the mid-seventeenth century.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Portuguese fort and presidio of Ambaca opens the inland route towards the Mbangala and the upper Kwango.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Arguin, the oldest Portuguese factory on the West African coast, is established in the 1440s on the Mauritanian shore and held until the Dutch take it in the 1630s.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Afro-Portuguese from Luanda settle at Benguela (map location Mbegela) from 1615, and Benguela becomes Portugal's second Angolan port, serving the Ovimbundu and southern caravan routes.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Bissau becomes the principal Portuguese fort and port of Guinea-Bissau from the late seventeenth century.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 10 'Senegambia from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century: evolution of the Wolof, Sereer and Tukuloor'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Cacheu, on the Rio Cacheu in Guinea-Bissau, is one of the earliest Portuguese trading stations of Upper Guinea and remains a Portuguese post to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 26 'Africa in inter-continental relations'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Cape Verde is settled from 1462 on the Madeira model, with Santiago the capital and residence of the governors; the islands remain Portuguese.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 13 'The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Portugal builds Sao Jorge da Mina castle at Elmina in 1482 and keeps a resident garrison and trading community there until the Dutch capture the castle in 1637; sovereignty over the surrounding Akan town is not claimed.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Paulo Dias de Novais founds Luanda in 1576 as the capital of Portuguese Angola, displacing the Afro-Portuguese traders of Sao Tome.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Fort Jesus, Mombasa'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1295/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Portugal builds Fort Jesus at Mombasa at the end of the sixteenth century (1593-96) and holds the port until the Omani siege of 1696-98.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Island of Mozambique'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/599/
facts.fact: Mozambique Island becomes the first seat of Portuguese colonial government in East Africa from 1507, held to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Portuguese forts on the Kwanza river at Muxima and Cambambe secure the route from Luanda to the interior.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 19 'The Kongo kingdom and its neighbours'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Portuguese storm the rock fortress of Pungo Andongo in 1671, destroying the last independent Ndongo kingdom.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Quelimane becomes a Portuguese port at the mouth of the Zambezi, outlet for the prazo estates of the lower river.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 26 'Africa in inter-continental relations'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Portugal settles Sao Tome in the 1490s; the island becomes a sugar and slave-trade base off the Gulf of Guinea and stays Portuguese to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Sena on the Zambezi, a Portuguese trading post and later prazo centre on the route to the Mutapa gold fields.

facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Island of Mozambique'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/599/ ; UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Portugal builds the fort of Sofala in 1505 and holds the old gold port, the southern anchor of its Zambezi and Mozambique coast.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 25 'East Africa: the coast'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Portuguese feiras at Sena and Tete on the Zambezi, established in the 1530s, are the inland limit of Portuguese settlement in the sixteenth century.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 22 'Southern Zambezia'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Changamire Dombo builds the Rozvi empire between 1684 and 1695 out of the Karanga of the old Mutapa state, with its capitals in the Changamire country (Dhlo-Dhlo, Danangombe).

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 22 'Southern Zambezia'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: The Changamire country around Khami and Dhlo-Dhlo, from which Dombo expelled the Portuguese and their feiras in the 1690s.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 12 'From the Niger to the Volta'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Segou's core territory on the Niger around Segou, held by the Coulibaly dynasty and its successors.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 12 'From the Niger to the Volta'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Biton Coulibaly builds the Bamana kingdom of Segou on the middle Niger in the early eighteenth century, with its capital at Segou.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 22 'The Sokoto caliphate and Borno'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Modibo Adama leads the jihad into Adamawa from 1809, bringing the upper Benue into the Sokoto caliphate as its easternmost emirate.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 22 'The Sokoto caliphate and Borno'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Uthman dan Fodio launches the jihad in Gobir in 1804; the caliphate is consolidated at Sokoto, and its emirs rule the central Sudan to the end of the period.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 22 'The Sokoto caliphate and Borno'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: By January 1809 all the main Hausa states had capitulated to the jihad; their capitals (Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir's Alkalawa, Kebbi) became emirates of the caliphate.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 22 'The Sokoto caliphate and Borno'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Ilorin, a northern Yoruba frontier town of Old Oyo, passes to the Sokoto caliphate after the Fulbe takeover of the 1820s and becomes its southernmost emirate.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 8 'The Songhay from the 12th to the 16th century'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Sonni Ali of Songhay takes Timbuktu from its Tuareg garrison in 1468; the town stays under Songhay until the Moroccan conquest of 1591.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century (1984), ch. 8 'The Songhay from the 12th to the 16th century'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_iv
facts.fact: Songhay absorbs the middle Niger towns of the Timbuktu area (Djenne after a long siege, c.1473; Macina) under Sonni Ali and keeps them until 1591.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 5 'The Mfecane and the rise of new African states'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: The Thaba Bosiu plateau and the surrounding Caledon valley, Moshoeshoe's base.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 5 'The Mfecane and the rise of new African states'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Moshoeshoe gathers the survivors of the Mfecane at Butha-Buthe and then, in 1824, at the mountain fortress of Thaba Bosiu, founding the Sotho kingdom.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 14 'The Sudan in the nineteenth century'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Muhammad Ali's army conquers the Funj sultanate in 1821 and rules the Gezira and the Nile valley from Khartoum; Kordofan is taken in the same campaign.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 17 'Kanem-Borno: its relations with the Mediterranean Sea, Bagirmi and other states in the Chad basin'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Wadai's core territory in the eastern Chad basin, taken from the Tunjur and Daju chiefs of the region.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (1992), ch. 17 'Kanem-Borno: its relations with the Mediterranean Sea, Bagirmi and other states in the Chad basin'; https://archive.org/details/unesco_general_history_africa_v
facts.fact: Abd al-Karim, a Maba prince educated in Borno, founds the sultanate of Wadai around 1635, with its capital at Ouara.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 5 'The Mfecane and the rise of new African states'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: The Zulu heartland in Natal and Zululand, the core of Shaka's and Dingane's kingdom.

facts.source: UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. VI: Africa in the Nineteenth Century until the 1880s (1989), ch. 5 'The Mfecane and the rise of new African states'; https://archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi
facts.fact: Shaka succeeds to the small Zulu chiefdom, takes over the Mthethwa confederacy after Dingiswayo's death in 1818, defeats the Ndwandwe and builds the Zulu kingdom.

facts.fact: English occupation of Normandy from the conquest of Rouen (1419) to the French reconquest completed in 1450.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'normandia': Normandy was definitively reconquered by Charles VII after the battle of Formigny (1450); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/normandia/

facts.fact: Charles VII completes the reconquest of Normandy in 1450; the duchy stays with the French crown.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'normandia': Riconquistata definitivamente da Carlo VII dopo la battaglia di Formigny (1450); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/normandia/

facts.fact: The French recovery of 1453 ends English rule in Gascony and Guyenne; only Calais remains English.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'francia': La pace del 1453 ridusse il dominio inglese in F. alla sola Calais; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/francia/

facts.fact: Brittany is bound to the French crown through the marriage of Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII (1491) and formally united in 1532.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'bretagna': il matrimonio dell'erede Anna con Carlo VIII (1491) unì la Bretagna alla Corona di Francia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/bretagna/

facts.fact: Louis XI takes over Provence on the death of its last Angevin count (1480-81); Nice is excluded because it had passed to Savoy in 1388.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'francia': Luigi XI (1461-83) occupò la Borgogna e la Provenza (1480); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/francia/

facts.fact: Savoy acquires Nice and its county in 1388 and holds it through the end of the period.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'savoia': ebbe la dedizione di Nizza e della relativa contea (1388); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/savoia/

facts.fact: Philip the Bold inherits Flanders in 1384 and adds it to the Burgundian lands.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': Filippo l'Ardito aggiunse nel 1384 alla Borgogna la Fiandra, la Franca Contea, l'Artois; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: Artois enters the Burgundian inheritance in 1384.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': Filippo l'Ardito aggiunse nel 1384 alla Borgogna la Fiandra, la Franca Contea, l'Artois; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: The county of Burgundy (Franche-Comte) passes to Philip the Bold in 1384.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': Filippo l'Ardito aggiunse nel 1384 alla Borgogna la Fiandra, la Franca Contea, l'Artois; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: Brabant is secured by Philip the Good in 1430 and incorporated in the Burgundian state.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brabante': solo nel 1430 la lotta per il dominio sul ducato terminò a favore dei Borgognoni; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brabante/

facts.fact: Hainaut passes to Burgundy with the Bavarian inheritance of Jacqueline of Hainaut in 1433.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': the Burgundian dukes extended their rule over the Low Countries in the 15th century; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: Holland, Zeeland and Frisia pass to Burgundy in 1433 after the abdication of Jacqueline of Bavaria.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': the Burgundian dukes extended their rule over the Low Countries in the 15th century; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: On the death of Charles the Bold in 1477 Louis XI occupies the duchy of Burgundy.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': dopo la sua morte Luigi XI re di Francia occupò il ducato; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: Maximilian of Habsburg takes the Burgundian Low Countries on the death of Charles the Bold in 1477.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'borgogna': la Franca Contea e i Paesi Bassi passarono a Massimiliano d'Asburgo; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/borgogna/

facts.fact: On Charles V's abdication in 1556 the Burgundian Low Countries pass to the Spanish branch of the Habsburgs.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brabante': alla morte dell'imperatore Carlo V, alla Spagna; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brabante/

facts.fact: The northern provinces abjure Philip II in 1581; the Union of Utrecht of 1579 is the constitutional basis of the Dutch Republic.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'utrecht': Unione di U.: conclusa il 23 gennaio 1579 ... statuto fondamentale della Repubblica delle Province Unite; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/utrecht/

facts.fact: The southern provinces (Brabant, Flanders, Wallonia) remain under the Spanish Habsburgs after the northern revolt.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brabante': il B. passò nel 1477 agli Asburgo e, alla morte di Carlo V, alla Spagna; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brabante/

facts.fact: By the treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt (1713-14) the Spanish Netherlands pass to the Austrian Habsburgs.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'utrecht': Utrecht 1713: the peace settlements transferred the Spanish Netherlands to the Austrian Habsburgs; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/utrecht/

facts.fact: Revolutionary France annexes the southern Netherlands in 1795; the annexation lasts until 1814-15.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'belgio': le province belghe furono unite a quelle olandesi nel regno dei Paesi Bassi (1815); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/belgio/

facts.fact: Belgium separates from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1830.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'belgio': Lo Stato belga venne costituito ufficialmente nel 1830-31; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/belgio/

facts.fact: The new Belgian kingdom takes over the southern provinces of the former Austrian/Spanish Netherlands.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'belgio': rivoluzione del 1830, che diede vita al Regno del Belgio; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/belgio/

Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'utrecht' (Unione di Utrecht, 23 January 1579, fundamental statute of the Republic of the United Provinces); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/utrecht/
facts.fact: The seven northern provinces abjure Philip II in 1581 and constitute the Dutch Republic, governed from The Hague.
The marriage of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon (1479) joins the two crowns; Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearics are ruled from Castile.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'spagna': Con la vittoria definitiva di Isabella (1479) ... essendo in quello stesso anno salito al trono di Aragona il marito Ferdinando, si venne a realizzare l'unione delle due corone; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/spagna/

facts.fact: Sardinia passes with the Aragonese inheritance to the united Spanish crown in 1479.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'sardegna': il trattato di Utrecht (1713) assegnò la Sardegna all'imperatore; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/sardegna/

facts.fact: The conquest of Granada in 1492 ends Muslim rule in Iberia and adds the emirate to Castile.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'spagna': la dominazione [musulmana] destinata a durare fino al 1492; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/spagna/

facts.fact: Ferdinand the Catholic conquers Spanish Navarre in 1512; the small trans-Pyrenean part stays with the Albret kings.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'navarra': Nel 1512 Ferdinando il Cattolico conquistò tutta la Navarra spagnola; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/navarra/

facts.fact: Lower Navarre is united with the French crown by Henry IV, formally in 1607.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'navarra': il cui ultimo re Enrico III, salito sul trono di Francia con il nome di Enrico IV (1589), riunì con atto formale (1607) l'avito possesso alla corona di Francia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/navarra/

facts.fact: Philip II of Spain is recognized as king of Portugal in 1580; the union lasts until the Portuguese restoration of 1640.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'portogallo': Nel 1580 ... prevalse il re di Spagna Filippo II; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/portogallo/

facts.fact: The Braganza restoration of 1640 returns Portugal to independence.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'portogallo': Nel 1640 ... nobiltà e borghesia si sollevarono, acclamando re il duca di Braganza; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/portogallo/

facts.fact: Philip II moves the Spanish court to Madrid in 1561, making it the capital.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'madrid': Nel 1561 Filippo II vi trasferì la corte, facendone la capitale dell'impero spagnolo; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/madrid/

facts.fact: Anglo-Dutch forces take Gibraltar in 1704; the treaty of Utrecht (1713) assigns it to the British crown.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'gibilterra': Nel 1713 il trattato di Utrecht la assegnò all'Inghilterra; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/gibilterra/

facts.fact: Alfonso of Aragon takes Naples in 1442-43; on his death in 1458 the kingdom passes to a cadet Aragonese line.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': Nel 1443 Alfonso d'Aragona entrò a Napoli; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: Ferdinand I, a cadet of the Aragonese house, rules Naples from 1458 to 1501.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': L'avvento degli Aragonesi, presto a Napoli rappresentati da un ramo cadetto; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: After the Franco-Spanish war of 1502-04 the kingdom of Naples remains to Spain (armistice of Lyon, 1504).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': il regno fu conteso fra i due vincitori, e alla fine rimase alla Spagna; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: Naples becomes an Austrian Habsburg possession in 1707.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': Divenuto nel 1707 possesso austriaco; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: Charles of Bourbon is installed as king of Naples in 1734.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': nel 1734 il regno fu ricostituito in favore di Carlo di Borbone; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: By the treaty of Utrecht (1713) Sicily goes to Savoy, which exchanges it for Sardinia in 1720.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'sardegna': con il trattato di Londra (1718) la Sardegna passò a Vittorio Amedeo II di Savoia ... nel 1720; all'Aia è fissato anche lo scambio; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/sardegna/

facts.fact: Sicily passes to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1720 in exchange for Sardinia.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'sardegna': all'Aia è fissato anche lo scambio [Sicily for Sardinia] (1720); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/sardegna/

facts.fact: Sicily follows the Aragonese crown into the Spanish union of 1479.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'spagna': 1479: unione delle corone di Castiglia e Aragona; la Sicilia seguì le sorti aragonesi; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/spagna/

facts.fact: Sicily is reunited with the Neapolitan crown under the Bourbons from 1734.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'napoli': nel 1734 il regno fu ricostituito in favore di Carlo di Borbone; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/napoli/

facts.fact: Savoy takes possession of Sardinia in 1720; the title of king of Sardinia remains with the house of Savoy.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'sardegna': la Sardegna passò a Vittorio Amedeo II di Savoia, che prese possesso dell'isola nel 1720; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/sardegna/

facts.fact: Louis XII takes Milan in 1499; the French hold the duchy until the Swiss restore the Sforza in 1512.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'milano': Nel 1499 entrarono a Milano i Francesi di Luigi XII; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/milano/

facts.fact: The Sforza are restored in Milan in 1512 and hold the duchy until 1535.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'milano': M. era quindi nuovamente dei Francesi, fino al 10 giugno 1512 quando essi la consegnarono alle truppe svizzere; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/milano/

facts.fact: On the death of the last Sforza duke in 1535 Milan passes to Charles V and then to the Spanish Habsburgs.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'milano': Nel 1535, morto lo Sforza, Milano e il ducato entrarono a far parte dei domini asburgici; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/milano/

facts.fact: Austrian troops take Milan in 1706; the duchy is formally ceded to Austria in 1713-14.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lombardia': Nel 18° sec., sotto gli Austriaci ...; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lombardia/

facts.fact: Revolutionary France organizes Lombardy into the Cisalpine Republic (1797) and later the Kingdom of Italy.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'milano': M. divenne la capitale della Repubblica Cisalpina (1797); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/milano/

facts.fact: The Restoration returns Lombardy to Austria in 1814-15 as part of the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lombardia': la Restaurazione del 1815 vide l'unione con Venezia nel Regno Lombardo-Veneto; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lombardia/

facts.fact: Venice conquers Padua and Verona (1404-05), then the patriarchate of Aquileia (1418-20) and Brescia and Bergamo (1428), creating its mainland dominion.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'venezia': Venezia conquistò Padova e Verona (1404-05) ... La Pace di Ferrara (1428) portò Brescia e Bergamo ... si impossessò del patriarcato di Aquileia (1418-20); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/venezia/

facts.fact: By the treaty of Campoformio (1797) Venice and its mainland pass to Austria.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'venezia': Con il Trattato di Campoformio (1797) Venezia fu ceduta all'Austria; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/venezia/

facts.fact: Florence takes Pisa in 1406, gaining direct access to the sea.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'firenze': Firenze ottiene, finalmente, Pisa; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/firenze/

facts.fact: Siena surrenders in 1555 and is ceded to Cosimo I de' Medici, joining the Florentine state.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'siena': S. si arrese nel 1555 ... fu investito del dominio senese il principe Filippo di Spagna che lo cedette a Cosimo I; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/siena/

facts.fact: Tuscany is reorganized under French control from 1801 (Kingdom of Etruria, then directly annexed in 1807-09).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'toscana': the grand duchy of Tuscany was reorganized under French control after 1801; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/toscana/

facts.fact: The Habsburg-Lorraine grand duchy of Tuscany is restored in 1814.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'toscana': the Habsburg-Lorraine grand duchy was restored in 1814; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/toscana/

facts.fact: The papal court returns from Avignon to Rome in 1377, which again becomes the seat of the papacy.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'avignone': Ma ritornata la corte pontificia a Roma (1377); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/avignone/

facts.fact: Genoa cedes Corsica to France by the treaty of Versailles (1768); the island stays French.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'corsica': Genova ... cedette i propri diritti in cambio di sussidi finanziari (trattato di Versailles, 1768); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/corsica/

facts.fact: Amadeus VIII extends Savoyard rule over Piedmont in the early 15th century; Turin becomes the capital in 1563.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'savoia': Amedeo VIII nel 1416 ebbe il titolo ducale; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/savoia/

facts.fact: Emmanuel Philibert moves the Savoyard capital from Chambery to Turin in 1563.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'torino': il duca vi entrò il 7 febbraio 1563 e vi stabilì definitivamente la capitale dello Stato piemontese; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/torino/

facts.fact: The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-36 annexes the principality and the marcher lordships to the realm of England.
facts.source: Legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives), Laws in Wales Act 1535 (27 Hen. 8 c. 26), Acts of the English Parliament; https://www.legislation.gov.uk/aep/Hen8/27/26

facts.fact: James VI of Scotland succeeds to the English throne in 1603; no monarch resides in Scotland thereafter, and the kingdoms are formally united in 1707.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'scozia': L'unione personale tra le corone di Scozia e d'Inghilterra [1603] non pose fine ai contrasti; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/scozia/

facts.fact: The submission of the Ulster lords in 1603 ends the Nine Years' War and brings Ulster under direct English crown government.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'irlanda': L'avvento al trono inglese di Giacomo I (1603) vide l'instaurazione di un centralismo amministrativo più accentuato; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/irlanda/

facts.fact: The Cromwellian conquest and the Act of Settlement of 1652 complete English control of the rest of Ireland.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'irlanda': Con l'Act of settlement (1652) furono confiscati circa 11 milioni di acri; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/irlanda/

facts.fact: The Union of Kalmar (1397) places Sweden under Danish kings; Sweden detaches itself again from 1448.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'danimarca': Nel 1397, la regina Margherita costituì l'unione di Kalmar fra i tre regni di Danimarca, Norvegia e Svezia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/danimarca/

facts.fact: Norway is ruled by Danish kings from 1380 without a resident monarch of its own; the union lasts until 1814.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'norvegia': Olaf dal 1380 re di Danimarca e di Norvegia ... La Norvegia e la Danimarca rimasero unite; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/norvegia/

facts.fact: The peace of Kiel (1814) transfers Norway from Denmark to Sweden; Norway keeps its own constitution in a personal union.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'norvegia': ottenne con la pace di Kiel (1814) la cessione della Norvegia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/norvegia/

facts.fact: The peace of Roskilde (1658) makes Scania part of Sweden.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'svezia': la Scania, fino allora danese, divenne parte integrante della Svezia con la pace di Roskilde (1658); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/svezia/

facts.fact: The Second Peace of Thorn (1466) takes western (Royal) Prussia from the Teutonic Order and gives it to Poland, which holds it until the First Partition (1772).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'prussia': la seconda pace di Thorn (1466) ... all'Ordine restò la Prussia orientale (con capitale Königsberg); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/prussia/

facts.fact: After 1466 the Order keeps only eastern Prussia as a Polish fief.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'prussia': all'Ordine restò la Prussia orientale (con capitale Königsberg), soggetta però all'alta signoria polacca; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/prussia/

facts.fact: Albert of Hohenzollern secularizes the Prussian Order state in 1525 as the hereditary Duchy of Prussia.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'prussia': Quando il gran maestro dell'Ordine Alberto di Hohenzollern aderì alla Riforma di Lutero, i possessi dell'Ordine, soppresso, si ridussero a un ducato laico ereditario; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/prussia/

facts.fact: The duchy comprises the former Order's eastern Prussian lands.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'prussia': ducato laico ereditario ... P. ducale; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/prussia/

facts.fact: On the extinction of the Prussian Hohenzollerns in 1618 their duchy passes to the elector of Brandenburg.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brandeburgo': Nel 1618 ... con l'estinzione del ramo degli Hohenzollern di Prussia, quel ducato [passò all'elettore di Brandeburgo]; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brandeburgo/

facts.fact: Prussia conquers Silesia in the First Silesian War (1742); the cession is confirmed at Aix-la-Chapelle (1748), except Troppau and Teschen.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'slesia': con il trattato di Aquisgrana (1748) passò alla Prussia (eccetto Troppau e Teschen); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/slesia/

facts.fact: Ferdinand of Austria is elected king of Bohemia in 1526; Bohemia and Moravia stay with the Habsburgs.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'boemia': Salito al trono (29 ott. 1526) Ferdinando d'Austria fratello di Carlo V, la Boemia passò agli Asburgo; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/boemia/

facts.fact: After the battle of Mohacs (1526) the Habsburgs are elected in the north and west of Hungary (Royal Hungary); the Ottoman-held centre and south are outside this fact.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'ungheria': Le lotte fra il partito nazionale, che elesse al trono Giovanni Szapolyai (1526-40), e i partigiani di Ferdinando d'Asburgo; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/ungheria/

facts.fact: The Union of Lublin (1569) merges the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lituania': L'unione ... perfezionata con gli atti di ... Lublino (1569); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lituania/

facts.fact: The Swiss Confederation is de facto independent of the Empire after the peace of Basel (1499).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'svizzera': con la pace di Basilea (1499) si emancipò di fatto definitivamente dall'Impero; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/svizzera/

facts.fact: The cantons of the old Confederation pass from Habsburg overlordship to the Confederation after 1499.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'svizzera': si ebbero così i 13 cantoni, che costituirono fino al 1798 l'antica Confederazione; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/svizzera/

facts.fact: On the death of Stanislas Leszczynski in 1766 Lorraine is annexed to France, as arranged in the 1738 treaty of Vienna.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lorena_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)': Alla morte del duca (1766) fu proclamata l'annessione alla Francia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lorena_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)/

facts.fact: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) gives France the Habsburg landgravates of Upper and Lower Alsace.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'alsazia': le paci di Vestfalia diedero (1648) alla Francia i langraviati dell'Alta e Bassa Alsazia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/alsazia/

facts.fact: Louis XIV annexes the Franche-Comte in 1668 and keeps it definitively from the peace of Nijmegen (1678).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'francia': Luigi ottenne numerose città fiamminghe e la Franca Contea (1668; 1678); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/francia/

facts.fact: The peace of the Pyrenees (1659) cedes Artois to France.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'spagna': con la pace dei Pirenei (1659) furono costretti ad abbandonare alla Francia l'Artois; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/spagna/

facts.fact: The peace of the Pyrenees (1659) cedes Roussillon and Cerdagne to France.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'spagna': con la pace dei Pirenei (1659) ... il Rossiglione e la Cerdaña; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/spagna/

facts.fact: The Peace of Westphalia gives Sweden the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, i.e. the mouth of the Weser and Elbe.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brema_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)': le pretese imperialistiche della Svezia che, ottenuto nel 1648 il dominio sulla foce del Weser; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brema_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)/

facts.fact: Swedish rule at the mouth of the Elbe and Weser ends with the cession of Bremen-Verden to Hanover in 1719.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brema_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)': sia per la caduta del dominio svedese sulle foci dell'Elba; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brema_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)/

facts.fact: The Act of Supremacy (1534) makes the king supreme head of the Church of England, separate from Rome.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'enrico-viii-re-d-inghilterra': Nel 1534 uscì dalla Chiesa di Roma e diede vita alla Chiesa anglicana, di cui si fece proclamare capo; l'atto di supremazia dello stesso anno completò la separazione della Chiesa inglese da Roma; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/enrico-viii-re-d-inghilterra/

facts.fact: The Västerås riksdag (1527) begins the Lutheran reformation of Sweden; the church is fully reformed by the 1530s.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'svezia': Dall'introduzione del protestantesimo (1527); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/svezia/

facts.fact: Christian III carries through the Lutheran reformation in Denmark-Norway in 1536.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'danimarca': Con la riforma luterana del re Cristiano III nel 1536; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/danimarca/

facts.fact: Ducal Prussia is the first territory to adopt Lutheranism as its official religion (1525).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'prussia': Quando il gran maestro dell'Ordine Alberto di Hohenzollern aderì alla Riforma di Lutero; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/prussia/

facts.fact: Brandenburg adopts the Lutheran reformation under Joachim II (1539-40).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'brandeburgo': Sotto il successore Gioacchino II (1535-71) il Brandeburgo accolse la riforma luterana; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/brandeburgo/

facts.fact: Hussite Bohemia maintains a separate utraquist church under the Compactata from the Hussite wars until the Catholic reconquest after 1620.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'boemia': Concluse queste con i compactata o articoli di Praga, con i quali i Boemi vennero riammessi nella Chiesa cattolica; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/boemia/

facts.fact: After the battle of the White Mountain (1620) the Habsburgs impose Catholicism on Bohemia.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'boemia': Ferdinando II (1620-37) impose loro una violenta controriforma; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/boemia/

facts.fact: The Dutch Republic adopts Calvinism as its public church from the Union of Utrecht and the Act of Abjuration.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'utrecht': Unione di Utrecht ... costituì lo statuto fondamentale della Repubblica delle Province Unite; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/utrecht/

facts.fact: The Scottish parliament abolishes papal authority and adopts the Calvinist confession in 1560.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'scozia': il Parlamento adottò la fede calvinista e nel 1567 costrinse la cattolica Maria ad abdicare; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/scozia/

facts.fact: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) gives Sweden western Pomerania with Rugen and Stettin.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'pomerania': il trattato di Vestfalia (1648) ... riconobbe il possesso del ducato, compresi l'isola di Rügen e Stettino, alla Svezia, mentre al Brandeburgo rimase la Pomerania orientale (Hinterpommern); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/pomerania/

facts.fact: Brandenburg keeps eastern (Further) Pomerania under the Westphalia settlement.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'pomerania': il trattato di Vestfalia (1648) ... riconobbe il possesso del ducato, compresi l'isola di Rügen e Stettino, alla Svezia, mentre al Brandeburgo rimase la Pomerania orientale (Hinterpommern); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/pomerania/

facts.fact: The peace of Stockholm (1721) and the congress of Vienna (1815) give Prussia the former Swedish Pomerania.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'pomerania': Con la pace di Stoccolma (1721) la Prussia ottenne la maggior parte della Pomerania svedese; con il trattato di Vienna (1815) ... il rimanente; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/pomerania/

facts.fact: Copenhagen becomes the capital of the Danish kingdom in 1443.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'copenaghen': nel 1443, divenne la capitale del Regno di Danimarca; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/copenaghen/

facts.fact: Berlin becomes the residence of the electors of Brandenburg in 1486.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'berlino': la loro importanza si accrebbe quando divennero residenza dei principi elettori di Brandeburgo (1486); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/berlino/

facts.fact: The Italian states maintain permanent resident embassies with one another from the mid-15th century until the French invasion of 1494.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'diplomazia_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)': In Italia si elaborano quelle istituzioni ... verso la metà del sec. XV, in una ventina circa di stati ... Col sec. XVI, si può dire abbia inizio la regolarità dei rapporti diplomatici tra i maggiori stati europei; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/diplomazia_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)/

facts.fact: Permanent resident diplomacy becomes standard among the major Latin Christian courts from about 1500.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'diplomazia_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)': In Italia si elaborano quelle istituzioni ... verso la metà del sec. XV, in una ventina circa di stati ... Col sec. XVI, si può dire abbia inizio la regolarità dei rapporti diplomatici tra i maggiori stati europei; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/diplomazia_(Enciclopedia-Italiana)/

facts.fact: The congress of Vienna (1815) unites the former Austrian Netherlands with the Dutch kingdom.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'belgio': Al Congresso di Vienna (1815) le province belghe furono unite a quelle olandesi nel regno dei Paesi Bassi; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/belgio/

facts.fact: After the war of the Spanish succession Mantua passes to the Austrian Habsburgs (1708), later administered with Milan.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lombardia': si unì al Mantovano (1708) che passò amministrativamente alle dipendenze di Milano (1737); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lombardia/

facts.fact: Savoy acquires the Novarese and Lomellina east of the Ticino from the Spanish succession settlements (1713).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'lombardia': passate ai Savoia (1713, 1735-48); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/lombardia/

facts.fact: The congress of Vienna (1815) assigns the former Genoese republic (Liguria) to the kingdom of Sardinia.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'genova' (Genoa's independence ends in 1797; the Ligurian territory is assigned to the kingdom of Sardinia in the 1815 settlement); https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/genova/

facts.fact: Iceland passes with Norway to the Danish crown at the end of the 14th century.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'danimarca': Nel 1397 ... fra i tre regni di Danimarca, Norvegia (ne dipendeva anche l'Islanda) e Svezia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/danimarca/

facts.fact: Edinburgh replaces Dunfermline as the habitual seat of the Scottish court in the 15th century (James II's reign).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'scozia': Edimburgo ... capitale; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/scozia/

facts.fact: Charles V grants Malta to the Knights of St John in 1530; they rule the island until 1798.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'malta': Nel 1530 fu concessa da Carlo V all'Ordine di S. Giovanni; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/malta/

facts.fact: Malta passes under British protection from 1800 and is confirmed as a British possession in 1814.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'malta': la conquista francese (1798) ... pose fine al dominio dei Cavalieri; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/malta/

facts.fact: In 1792 revolutionary France annexes Savoy and Nice; the territories are restored to Savoy in 1814.
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'savoia': Vittorio Amedeo III cedette alla Francia Nizza e la Savoia; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/savoia/

facts.fact: The Restoration returns Savoy, Nice and Piedmont to the house of Savoy (1814-15).
facts.source: Treccani, Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana, entry 'savoia': Abbattuta la repubblica piemontese ... [the Restoration]; https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/savoia/

facts.fact: Electoral Saxony becomes the Lutheran stronghold of the Empire from the mid-1520s.
