facts.fact: Paul I, heir to Catherine II from 1762 and emperor from 1796, married Wilhelmina, daughter of Louis IX Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt, an Imperial immediate landgraviate, at St Petersburg on 10 October 1773; the marriage ended at her death in childbirth on 26 April 1776.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "RUSSIA, Rurik" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m firstly (St Petersburg 10 Oct 1773) WILHELMINE Landgräfin von Hessen-Darmstadt, daughter of LUDWIG IX Landgraf von Hessen-Darmstadt ... (Prenzlau 25 Jun 1755-St Petersburg 26 Apr 1776)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/RUSSIA,%20Rurik.htm

facts.fact: Paul I married secondly Sophie Dorothea, daughter of Friedrich Eugen Duke of Württemberg (a sovereign Imperial duke), at St Petersburg on 7 October 1776; counted to his assassination on 24 March 1801.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "RUSSIA, Rurik" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m secondly (St Petersburg 7 Oct 1776) SOPHIE DOROTHEA Pss von Württemberg, daughter of FRIEDRICH EUGEN Herzog von Württemberg [later FRIEDRICH II EUGEN Herzog von Württemberg]"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/RUSSIA,%20Rurik.htm

facts.fact: Alexander I married Luise, daughter of Karl Ludwig Hereditary Margrave of Baden, at St Petersburg on 9 October 1793, but he was only the second in line until his father's accession made him heir in 1796; the marriage of a sovereign margrave's daughter is therefore counted from 1796 to his death on 1 December 1825.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "RUSSIA, Rurik" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m (St Petersburg 9 Oct 1793) LUISE Pss von Baden, daughter of KARL LUDWIG Erbmarkgraf von Baden ... (Karlsruhe 24 Jan 1779-Bielev, near Kaluga 16 May 1826)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/RUSSIA,%20Rurik.htm

facts.fact: Nicholas I married Charlotte, daughter of Frederick William III King of Prussia, at St Petersburg on 13 July 1817, but his elder brother Constantine stood ahead of him until 1825, so the marriage is counted from his accession in 1825 to the 1837 limit of this timeline.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "RUSSIA, Rurik" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m (St Petersburg 13 Jul 1817) CHARLOTTE Pss of Prussia, daughter of FRIEDRICH WILHELM III King of Prussia & his first wife Luise Pss von Mecklenburg-Strelitz"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/RUSSIA,%20Rurik.htm

facts.fact: Frederick I, King in Prussia from 18 January 1701, had married in 1684 Sophia Charlotte, daughter of Ernest Augustus Elector of Hanover, an Imperial electorate; counted from his coronation in 1701 to her death in 1705.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (ADB/NDB), 'Friedrich I.', s.v.: "F. war drei Mal vermählt. ... Die Ehe mit Sophie Charlotte von Hannover ging F. 1684 ein. Nach 21 Jahren (1705) wurde auch sie ihrem Gemahl entrissen"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz53015.html

facts.fact: Frederick I married thirdly in 1708 Sophia Louise, daughter of Christian Louis I Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin; counted from 1708 to his death on 25 February 1713.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (ADB/NDB), 'Friedrich I.', s.v.: "Seine dritte ihn überlebende Gemahlin, Sophie Luise von Mecklenburg, war bald nach der Vermählung (1708)"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz53015.html

facts.fact: Frederick William I, King in Prussia from 1713, had married Sophia Dorothea, daughter of George Louis Elector of Hanover (from 1714 King George I of Great Britain), on 26 November 1706; counted from his accession in 1713 to his death on 31 May 1740.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (ADB, NDB), 'Friedrich Wilhelm I.', s.v.: "Am 26. November 1706 vermählte sich F. W. mit Sophie Dorothea, der Tochter des Kurfürsten von Hannover, nachmaligen Königs von England"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz68348.html

facts.fact: Frederick II, crown prince from 1713 and king from 1740, was married at Salzdahlum in 1733 to Elisabeth Christine, daughter of Ferdinand Albert II Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg-Bevern; the childless marriage lasted to his death in 1786.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (NDB), 'Friedrich II.', genealogical heading: "⚭ Salzdahlum 1733 Elisabeth Christine (1715–97), T d. Hzg. Ferd. Albrecht II. v. Braunschweig-Lüneburg-Bevern (1680–1735); kinderlos"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz56983.html

facts.fact: Frederick William II, heir to the Prussian throne from 1758, married in 1765 Elisabeth Christine, daughter of Charles I Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg; the marriage was dissolved by judicial decree in 1769 and is counted only to that year.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (NDB), 'Friedrich Wilhelm II.', genealogical heading: "⚭ 1) 1765 (⚮ 1769) Elis. Christine (1746–1840), T d. Hzg. Karl I. v. Braunschweig-Lüneburg"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz53018.html

facts.fact: Frederick William II married secondly in 1769 Frederica Louisa, daughter of Louis IX Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt, an Imperial immediate landgraviate; the marriage lasted to his death on 16 November 1797.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (NDB), 'Friedrich Wilhelm II.', genealogical heading: "2) 1769 Frieder. Luise (1751–1805), T d. Landgf. Ludwig IX. v. Hessen-Darmstadt († 1790)"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz53018.html

facts.fact: Frederick William III, crown prince from 1786 and king from 1797, married Louise, daughter of Charles II Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, on 24 December 1793; counted to her death in 1810.
facts.source: Deutsche Biographie (ADB), 'Friedrich Wilhelm III.', s.v.: "Am 24. December 1793 vermählte sich der Kronprinz mit der schönen und hochherzigen Prinzessin Louise von Mecklenburg-Strelitz, geboren zu Hannover am 10. März 1776"; https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz56984.html

facts.fact: Orhan, Ottoman bey from 1326, married Theodora, daughter of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, in early summer 1346 at a ceremony outside Silivri; a reigning emperor's daughter, the match bought Orhan's support in the Byzantine civil war and lasted to his death in 1362.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m thirdly (early summer 1346) THEODORA Kantakuzene, daughter of Emperor IOANNES VI Kantakuzenos & his wife Eirene Asanina (-after May 1381)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm; Halil İnalcık, 'ORHAN', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi: "Kantakuzenos 1346'da kızı Theodora'yı zevce olarak Orhan'a verdi"; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/orhan

facts.fact: Murad I, sultan from 1362, took as wife Kera Tamara (Keratamas), daughter of Tsar Ivan Alexander Asen of Bulgaria, between 1371 and 1376; a reigning tsar's daughter given as part of Bulgaria's submission, the marriage lasted to his death at Kosovo on 15 June 1389.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m fourthly ([1371/76]) KERATAMAS [Tamara] of Bulgaria, daughter of IVAN ALEXANDER ASEN Tsar of the Bulgarians & his second wife Sarah [Teodora] ---. Laonicus Chalcocondylas records the marriage of 'Susmanum Mysiæ regem…filia' and 'Amuratem'"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Murad I married in 1383 a daughter of Süleyman Shah Pasha II, emir of Candar (Isfendiyar), a Turkmen beylik with its own 1337 tag on the map; the match was part of Murad's subjection of the Anatolian beyliks and ended at his death in 1389.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m sixthly (1383) ---, daughter of Amir Damad SÜLEYMAN Shah Pasha II Emir of Candar"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Bayezid I, then governor of Kütahya and heir of Murad I, married Devlet (Daulat) Shah, daughter of Süleyman Shah Chelebi emir of Germiyan, about 1378-1381, receiving Kütahya and other Germiyan districts as her dowry; Germiyan was a separate beylik with its own 1337 tag, and the marriage ended with his death in captivity in March 1403.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m thirdly (1378) DAULAT Shah, daughter of --- (Kutahya 1365-Bursa 1414)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm; Halil İnalcık, 'BAYEZİD I', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi: "1381 yılı dolaylarında Germiyanoğlu Süleyman (Şah) Çelebi'nin kızı Sultan Hatun ile evlendi ve hanımının çeyizi olarak Osmanlılar'a bırakılan topraklara sancak beyi tayin edildi"; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/bayezid-i

facts.fact: Bayezid I took as wife Hafisa Khanum, daughter of Fakhr ud-din Isa bey, emir of Aydın, a separate Turkmen beylik with its own 1337 tag; the marriage is undated within his princely years and is placed between 1378 and 1390, ending with his death in 1403.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m fifthly HAFISA Khanum, daughter of Amir FAKHR ud-din Isa bey Emir of Aydin"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Bayezid I married Olivera (Maria Despina), daughter of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović of Serbia, in 1390, the match arranged by her mother when Serbia accepted Ottoman suzerainty after Kosovo; Serbia was a separate principality and the marriage lasted to his death in 1403.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m eighthly (1390) OLIVERA of Serbia, daughter of LAZAR Hrebljanović Knez of Serbia & his wife Jelena --- (-after 1443). ... Her marriage was arranged by her mother when she accepted Ottoman suzerainty over Serbia in 1390"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Mehmed I, then a prince fighting for the Ottoman succession and sultan from 1413, married Emine (Amina) Khanum, daughter of Nasir ud-din Mehmed bey, emir of Dulkadir, in 1403; Dulkadir was a separate Turkmen principality with its own 1337 tag, and the marriage lasted to his death on 26 May 1421.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v. (Sultan Mohammed I): "m secondly (1403) AMINA Khanum, daughter of NASIR ud-din Muhammad bey Amir of Dulkadir (1389-1419)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm; TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'DULKADIROĞULLARI': "Kızlarından birini Osmanlı şehzadesi Çelebi Mehmed'e veren Nasreddin Mehmed Bey"; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/dulkadirogullari

facts.fact: Murad II, sultan from 1421, married Alima Khanum of the Dulkadir house as his first wife in 1421; a separate Turkmen principality with its own 1337 tag, the match lasted to his death on 13 February 1451.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m firstly (1421) ALIMA Khanum of Dulkadir"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Murad II married at Adrianople in 1423 Taj un-nisa Halima Khanum, daughter of Ibrahim II bey of Candar, a separate beylik with its own 1337 tag; the marriage lasted to his death in 1451.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m fifthly (Adrianople 1423) TAJ un-nisa Khadija HALIMA Khanum, daughter of Amir Damad TAJ ud-din Ibrahim II bey Amir of Candar"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Murad II betrothed Mara, daughter of Đurađ Branković Despot of Serbia, in June 1433 and married her at Adrianople on 4 September 1435, her dowry being the districts of Toplica and Dubočica; Serbia was a separate principality, and the marriage ended at his death in 1451.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v.: "m sixthly (betrothed Jun 1433, Adrianople 4 Sep 1435) MARA of Serbia, daughter of DJURADJ Vuković Despot of Serbia & his wife Eirene Kantakuzene ([1416/17]-Ježovo 14 Sep 1487)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm

facts.fact: Mehmed II, then a prince under his father Murad II and sultan from 1451, married Sitt Hatun (Sitti Mükrime), daughter of Süleyman bey of Dulkadir, in 1449 or 1450 (Süleyman gave her in the year after the 1449 Mamluk match); Dulkadir was a separate Turkmen principality with its own 1337 tag, and the marriage ended at her death in 1467.
facts.source: Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, Medieval Lands, "TURKS" (Charles Cawley, ed.), s.v. (Sultan Mohammed II): "m [secondly] (Sep 1449) SITT Hatun, daughter of Emir IBRAHIM ruler of the Dulkadirh Türkmen tribe in eastern Anatolia (-1467)"; https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/TURKS.htm; TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'DULKADIROĞULLARI': "ertesi yıl diğer kızı Sitti Hatun'u II. Murad'ın oğlu Şehzade Mehmed'e verdi"; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/dulkadirogullari

facts.fact: Bayezid II, prince of Amasya until 1481 and sultan from 1481, was married to a daughter of Alaüddevle Bozkurt bey of Dulkadir, who took that throne in 1480; a separate Turkmen principality with its own 1337 tag, the marriage is counted from about 1480 to his abdication in April 1512.
facts.source: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'DULKADIROĞULLARI': "Fâtih'in desteklediği Alâüddevle Bey 1480'de Şahbudak'ı yenerek Dulkadırlı tahtını ele geçirdi. Sultan II. Bayezid Alâüddevle'nin kızıyla evliydi"; https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/dulkadirogullari

facts.fact: Akbar, emperor from 1556, married in 1562 Mariam-uz-Zamani, daughter of Raja Bharmal of Amber, the Kachhwaha Rajput kingdom of Dhundhar, which is separately represented on the map by its own tag at its capital Amber (not held by Delhi); the alliance lasted to Akbar's death on 27 October 1605.
facts.source: Vincent A. Smith, Akbar the Great Mogul, 1542-1605 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1917), ch. 4: "in the middle of January 1562, he started for Ajmer ... he received Raja Bihar Mall, the chief of Amber or Jaipur ... who offered his eldest daughter to Akbar in marriage ... The marriage was celebrated at Sambhar. ... The bride subsequently became the mother of Jahangir"; https://archive.org/details/akbargreatmogul100smituoft; Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama, trans. H. Beveridge: "In order to do honour to Rajah Bhagwan Das, his auspicious sister, who held high rank in the imperial harem"; https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.236537

facts.fact: Akbar also married a princess of Jaisalmer, daughter of Rawal Harraj who had ruled that Rajput kingdom; the match is attested by the Akbarnama's notice of her daughter Mahi Begum, who died on 28 March 1577 aged about a year, described as the grandchild of Rawal Harraj the ruler of Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer is separately represented on the map by its own 1337 tag. The wedding year is unrecorded but must fall before the daughter's birth in about 1576; counted to Akbar's death in 1605.
facts.source: Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama, trans. H. Beveridge (Bibliotheca Indica): 'One of the occurrences was the departure of Mahi Begam to the spiritual world. That nursling of the rose garden of the Caliphate was the grand-child of Rawal Harraj the ruler of Jaisalmer ... she on 18 Parwardin, Divine month (28 March 1577), turned her face from the outer world, and did not gather flowers in a fading garden for a longer space than a year.' (editor's note: 'This was a daughter of Akbar'); https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.236537

facts.fact: Jahangir (Salim), eldest son of the reigning Akbar and emperor from 1605, married Man Bai (Shah Begum), daughter of Raja Bhagwant Das of Amber, on 13 February 1585; her Kachhwaha kingdom of Dhundhar has its own 1337 tag at Amber, and the marriage ended at her death on 5 May 1605.
facts.source: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. A. Rogers, ed. H. Beveridge, index s.v. "Shah Begam, title given to Khusrau's mother, daughter of Bhagwan Das"; https://archive.org/details/tuzukijahangirio00jahauoft; Wikipedia, 'Shah Begum (wife of Jahangir)' (m. 13 February 1585, d. 5 May 1605): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Begum_(wife_of_Jahangir)

facts.fact: Jahangir married Manavati Bai (Jagat Gosain, remembered as Jodh Bai), daughter of Raja Udai Singh of Marwar, on 21 January 1586, the mother of Shah Jahan; Marwar's Rathore state is separately represented on the map by the Marwari tag seated at Khed with Pali and Bahadamer, and the marriage ended at her death on 8 April 1619.
facts.source: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. A. Rogers, ed. H. Beveridge, p. 19: "To Jagat Gosa'in, daughter of the Mota Raja (the fat raja), was born Sultan Khurram"; https://archive.org/details/tuzukijahangirio00jahauoft; Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama, vol. 3: "Another daughter of the Mota Rajah ... was married to Jahangir in 994, 1586"; https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.236537

facts.fact: Aurangzeb, then a Mughal prince and emperor from 1658, married Rahmat-un-Nissa (Nawab Bai), daughter of Raja Tajuddin Khan, the Jarral ruler of Rajauri, in 1638; Rajauri is separately represented on the map by its own 1337 tag at Rajouri (not held by Delhi), and the marriage ended at her death about 1691.
facts.source: Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 1, ch. iii: "Rahmat-un-nisa, surnamed Nawab Bai, the mother of Bahadur Shah I ... was the daughter of Rajah Raju of the Rajauri State in Kashmir"; https://archive.org/details/aurangzeb-1-2-jadunath-sarkar_202110; Wikipedia, 'Nawab Bai' (married 1638, died c. 1691): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawab_Bai

facts.fact: Timur takes sovereign power at Balkh and rules from Samarkand; the Timurid line holds Khorasan from Herat until the Shaybanids take it in 1507.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Ismail I takes Tabriz and is crowned shah in 1501, founding the Safavid state; the same Iranian state continues through the Afsharid, Zand and Qajar dynasties.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: After the Zaydi tribes expel the Ottomans from the Yemeni highlands by 1635, the Qasimi imams rule from Sanaa.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdali sultanate; https://www.britannica.com/place/Abdali-sultanate

facts.fact: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and Muhammad ibn Saud establish the Saudi emirate at Diriyah in 1744; Ibrahim Pasha destroys it in 1818.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudi Arabia: history; https://www.britannica.com/place/Saudi-Arabia/History

facts.fact: The London Protocol of 1830 and the frontier settlement of 1832 create an independent Greek kingdom with Nafplio as its first capital.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, War of Greek Independence; https://www.britannica.com/event/War-of-Greek-Independence

facts.fact: French troops take Algiers on 5 July 1830 and establish a colonial administration that expands along the coast.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Algiers; https://www.britannica.com/place/Algiers

facts.fact: Orhan annexes the Karasi beylik of Balikesir after defeating its ruler; the Ottomans hold the district to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Orhan (Ottoman sultan); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Orhan ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Karasi dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Karasi-dynasty

facts.fact: Orhan takes Nicomedia (Izmit) and the Kocaeli peninsula, completing Ottoman control of the Marmara shore opposite Constantinople.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Orhan (Ottoman sultan); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Orhan

facts.fact: Orhan takes Ankara in 1354; the city is lost when Timur restores the Anatolian beyliks after the battle of Ankara in 1402.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Orhan (Ottoman sultan); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Orhan

facts.fact: Mehmed I re-establishes Ottoman rule in central Anatolia after the interregnum; Ankara remains Ottoman to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: Ottoman rule is restored across the Sivas-Kayseri-Amasya region during the reign of Mehmed I and consolidated under Murad II.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: Bayezid I annexes the western Anatolian beyliks of Aydin, Saruhan, Mentese, Hamid and Teke around 1390; Timur restores them in 1402.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Aydin dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Aydin-dynasty ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mentese dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mentese-dynasty ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hamid dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hamid-dynasty

facts.fact: The Saruhan beylik around Manisa is finally reincorporated into the Ottoman state when its last ruler is killed after the interregnum.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saruhan dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saruhan-dynasty

facts.fact: Murad II annexes the Aydin beylik of Birgi and Smyrna in 1425; Smyrna stays Ottoman to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Aydin dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Aydin-dynasty

facts.fact: The Mentese beylik of Mugla is annexed by Murad II in the mid-1420s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mentese dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mentese-dynasty

facts.fact: The Hamid beylik of Isparta is absorbed by Murad II in 1423.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hamid dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hamid-dynasty

facts.fact: Murad II annexes the Teke beylik centred on Antalya in 1423.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hamid dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hamid-dynasty

facts.fact: The Alaiye principality on the southern coast is annexed under Mehmed II, completing Ottoman control of the Antalya littoral.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Karaman; https://www.britannica.com/place/Karaman

facts.fact: The Germiyan beylik of Kutahya passes to the Ottomans by bequest and annexation in 1429.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: Mehmed II conquers the Karamanid emirate in 1468 after the death of Ibrahim Bey; Karamanid resistance in the Taurus continues into the 1480s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Karaman; https://www.britannica.com/place/Karaman

facts.fact: Mehmed II annexes the Candar (Isfendiyarid) principality of Kastamonu and Sinop in 1461, and the Genoese trading post of Amasra with it.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Candar dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Candar-dynasty

facts.fact: The Empire of Trebizond surrenders to Mehmed II in August 1461; the Pontic coast becomes an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Candar dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Candar-dynasty

facts.fact: Selim I defeats the Dulkadir principality at Turnadag in 1515; its territory around Maras and Malatya is fully incorporated after 1522.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Dulkadir dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Dulkadir-dynasty

facts.fact: The Ramazanoglu principality of Adana loses its hereditary autonomy and Cilicia becomes a directly administered Ottoman province in 1608.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Adana; https://www.britannica.com/place/Adana-Turkey

facts.fact: The Knights Hospitaller hold Smyrna after the 1344 crusade until Timur destroys their fortress in 1402.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Crusades: the later Crusades; https://www.britannica.com/event/Crusades/The-later-Crusades

facts.fact: Peter I of Cyprus takes and briefly holds Antalya (Satalia) on the Anatolian coast.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Peter I, king of Cyprus; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Peter-I-king-of-cyprus

facts.fact: The Genoese Maona company governs the island of Chios from the mid-fourteenth century until the Ottoman annexation in 1566.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Suleyman I annexes Genoese Chios in 1566 after the fall of the Maona administration.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Mehmed II takes Lesbos from the Gattilusio lords in 1462 and the northern Aegean islands pass under Ottoman rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: The Ottoman fleet takes Lemnos and Imbros after the fall of Lesbos in 1462.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Genoa occupies Famagusta after the Cypriot war with Peter II and holds the port until Venice takes Cyprus in 1489 and the Genoese garrison is expelled.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cyprus: Byzantine Empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Cyprus/Byzantine-Empire

facts.fact: Venice acquires Cyprus in 1489 when Caterina Cornaro cedes the kingdom to the Republic.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cyprus: Byzantine Empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Cyprus/Byzantine-Empire

facts.fact: Ottoman forces conquer Cyprus in 1570-71 and the island becomes an Ottoman province after the fall of Famagusta.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cyprus: Byzantine Empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Cyprus/Byzantine-Empire

facts.fact: Mehmed II takes Negroponte (Chalkis) from Venice in 1470, ending Venetian rule over Euboea.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: The Duchy of Naxos passes to Ottoman suzerainty under Joseph Nasi in 1566 and is directly administered after 1579.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Suleyman I captures Rhodes from the Knights Hospitaller after a five-month siege in 1522.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Siege of Rhodes; https://www.britannica.com/event/Siege-of-Rhodes

facts.fact: The Ottoman capital moves from Bursa to Edirne under Murad I.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Edirne; https://www.britannica.com/place/Edirne

facts.fact: Mehmed II moves the Ottoman capital from Edirne to Constantinople after the conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: After the battle of Maritsa in 1371 the Ottomans take the Maritsa valley and the Thracian hinterland of Edirne.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of the Maritsa River; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Maritsa-River

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of Macedonia proceeds from the capture of Serres in the early 1380s to the fall of Skopje in 1392.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of the Maritsa River; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Maritsa-River ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, North Macedonia: the Ottoman Empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Macedonia/The-Ottoman-Empire ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Serrai; https://www.britannica.com/place/Serrai

facts.fact: Murad II captures Thessaloniki from Venice in 1430, ending the city's period of Venetian rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Murad II; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Murad-II

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of Thessaly in 1393 ends the rule of the Serbian successor lords of Symeon Uros in the region.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Greece: Despotate of Epirus; https://www.britannica.com/place/Greece/Despotate-of-Epirus ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Symeon Uros; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Symeon-Uros

facts.fact: The Ottomans take Ioannina in 1430, ending the Despotate of Epirus in its southern core.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Greece: Despotate of Epirus; https://www.britannica.com/place/Greece/Despotate-of-Epirus

facts.fact: Arta, the last centre of the Despotate of Epirus, falls to the Ottomans in 1449.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Arta; https://www.britannica.com/place/Arta

facts.fact: Sofia is taken by the Ottomans in 1382, opening the way into the central Balkans.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bulgaria: the second Bulgarian empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bulgaria/The-second-Bulgarian-empire

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of the Bulgarian Tsardom is completed with the fall of Tarnovo in 1393.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bulgaria: the second Bulgarian empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bulgaria/The-second-Bulgarian-empire

facts.fact: The rump Bulgarian kingdom of Vidin is annexed in 1396.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Vidin; https://www.britannica.com/place/Vidin ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bulgaria: the second Bulgarian empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bulgaria/The-second-Bulgarian-empire

facts.fact: The Dobruja, contested between the Bulgarian despotate and Wallachia, passes under direct Ottoman rule by 1419.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Dobruja; https://www.britannica.com/place/Dobruja

facts.fact: The Serbian Despotate ends with the fall of Smederevo in 1459 and its territory becomes an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Serbia; https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Serbia ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Serbia: conquest by the Ottoman Turks; https://www.britannica.com/place/Serbia/Conquest-by-the-Ottoman-Turks

facts.fact: Suleyman I takes Belgrade in 1521; the fortress becomes the seat of an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Belgrade; https://www.britannica.com/place/Belgrade

facts.fact: The Habsburgs take Belgrade in 1717 and keep it under the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz

facts.fact: The Treaty of Belgrade in 1739 restores Belgrade and northern Serbia to the Ottoman Empire.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Belgrade (1739); https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Belgrade-1739

facts.fact: Matthias Corvinus takes Jajce in 1463 and the Hungarian banate of Jajce holds the fortress until its fall to the Ottomans in 1528.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Jajce; https://www.britannica.com/place/Jajce

facts.fact: After the Ottoman capture of Shkoder in 1479 the Albanian lands pass under direct Ottoman rule; Skanderbeg's resistance ends with the fall of Kruje.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Shkoder; https://www.britannica.com/place/Shkoder ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Skanderbeg; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Skanderbeg

facts.fact: Venice acquires Durres in 1392 and holds the port until the Ottomans take it in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Durres; https://www.britannica.com/place/Durres

facts.fact: The Ottomans capture Venetian Durres in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Durres; https://www.britannica.com/place/Durres

facts.fact: Shkoder is sold to Venice in 1396 and held by the Republic until its surrender to the Ottomans in 1479.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Shkoder; https://www.britannica.com/place/Shkoder

facts.fact: Venice rules Bar (Antivari) from 1443 until the Ottoman conquest in 1571.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bar (Montenegro); https://www.britannica.com/place/Bar-Montenegro

facts.fact: Kotor accepts Venetian rule in 1420 and remains part of Venetian Albania until the fall of the Republic in 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kotor; https://www.britannica.com/place/Kotor

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of the Despotate of the Morea in 1460 brings the Peloponnese under direct Ottoman rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Venice holds the ports of Modon and Coron in the southern Peloponnese until the Ottoman conquest of 1500.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Bayezid II takes Modon and Coron from Venice in 1500.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Venice holds Monemvasia from the 1460s until the Ottoman conquest of 1540.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Suleyman I takes Monemvasia and Nauplia from Venice in 1540.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Venice holds the island of Kythera off the southern Peloponnese to the end of the Republic.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of the Latin lordships of Athens and Neopatras in 1458 and of Aetolia completes Ottoman control of central Greece.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Corfu places itself under Venetian protection in 1386 and stays Venetian until 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Corfu; https://www.britannica.com/place/Corfu ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Zakynthos passes to Venice in 1485 and remains Venetian until 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Cephalonia passes to Venice in 1502 after the Ottoman occupation of 1479-1500.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cephallenia; https://www.britannica.com/place/Cephallenia

facts.fact: Venice takes Lefkada from the Ottomans in 1684 and holds it to 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Parga is held by Venice from the early fifteenth century until 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: The independent Greek kingdom established in 1830 takes over the Peloponnese with the Arta-Volos frontier of 1832.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, War of Greek Independence; https://www.britannica.com/event/War-of-Greek-Independence ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Greece: building the nation, 1832-1913; https://www.britannica.com/place/Greece/Building-the-nation-1832-1913

facts.fact: Attica, Boeotia and Aetolia join the Greek kingdom with the 1832 frontier settlement.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Greece: building the nation, 1832-1913; https://www.britannica.com/place/Greece/Building-the-nation-1832-1913

facts.fact: Nafplio serves as the first capital of the Greek kingdom until the court moves to Athens in 1834.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Otto, king of Greece; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Otto-king-of-Greece ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Greece: building the nation, 1832-1913; https://www.britannica.com/place/Greece/Building-the-nation-1832-1913

facts.fact: Mehmed II conquers the Kingdom of Bosnia in 1463; the area becomes the core of the Bosnian sanjak.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Balkans: the Ottomans; https://www.britannica.com/place/Balkans/The-Ottomans ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tvrtko I; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tvrtko-I

facts.fact: The Duchy of Saint Sava (Herzegovina) is annexed by the Ottomans in 1482, completing the conquest of the Bosnian lands.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Balkans: the Ottomans; https://www.britannica.com/place/Balkans/The-Ottomans

facts.fact: The Hungarian banate of Jajce falls to the Ottomans in 1527-28, ending Hungarian rule in central Bosnia.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Jajce; https://www.britannica.com/place/Jajce

facts.fact: Bihac, the last Croatian-Hungarian stronghold on the Una, falls to the Ottomans in 1592.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Balkans: the Ottomans; https://www.britannica.com/place/Balkans/The-Ottomans

facts.fact: Suleyman I occupies Buda in 1541 and the central Hungarian plain becomes an Ottoman province; Esztergom and Szekesfehervar follow in 1543.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Mohacs; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Mohacs

facts.fact: Eger falls in 1596 and Kanizsa in 1600, extending Ottoman rule to northern and south-western Hungary.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition

facts.fact: The Banat of Temesvar is conquered in 1552 and organised as a separate Ottoman province until the Habsburg conquest of 1716-18.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz

facts.fact: Ottoman raiders take Slavonia after 1540; the region is formally ceded to the Habsburgs at Karlowitz in 1699.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Carlowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Carlowitz

facts.fact: Buda is recaptured in 1686 and the Habsburgs take over central Hungary, confirmed at Karlowitz in 1699.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Carlowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Carlowitz

facts.fact: Eger surrenders in 1687 and Kanizsa in 1690, completing the Habsburg reconquest of northern and western Hungary.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition

facts.fact: Slavonia is formally transferred to the Habsburg monarchy by the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Carlowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Carlowitz

facts.fact: Eugene of Savoy takes Temesvar in 1716 and Austria keeps the Banat under the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz

facts.fact: The Principality of Transylvania passes from Ottoman suzerainty to the Habsburg monarchy at Karlowitz, after the Diploma Leopoldinum of 1690.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hungary: the period of partition; https://www.britannica.com/place/Hungary/The-period-of-partition ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diploma Leopoldinum; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Diploma-Leopoldinum

facts.fact: Habsburg forces occupy Oltenia (Little Wallachia) in 1718 and hold it until the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Belgrade (1739); https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Belgrade-1739

facts.fact: The Ottomans take Kilia and Cetatea Alba at the mouth of the Danube from Moldavia in 1484.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy

facts.fact: Cetatea Alba (Akkerman) passes to direct Ottoman rule with Kilia in 1484.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy

facts.fact: Suleyman I annexes Tighina (Bender) on the Dniester in 1538 and turns it into an Ottoman fortress.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy

facts.fact: Hotin is placed under direct Ottoman administration in 1713 after the removal of the Moldavian prince; Russia takes it in 1812.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bukovina; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bukovina

facts.fact: The southern Moldavian districts around Bender and the Budjak are detached from Moldavia and ruled directly by the Ottomans from 1538.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy

facts.fact: Selim I defeats the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in August 1516 and Syria and Palestine pass under Ottoman rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Marj Dabik; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Marj-Dabiq

facts.fact: Selim I defeats the Mamluks at Raydaniyya in January 1517 and Egypt becomes an Ottoman province; Muhammad Ali, viceroy from 1805, rules it as an autonomous but still Ottoman dependency.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Marj Dabik; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Marj-Dabiq

facts.fact: Muhammad Ali is appointed Ottoman viceroy of Egypt in 1805; his dynasty rules the province autonomously.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Egypt: Muhammad Ali and his successors; https://www.britannica.com/place/Egypt/Muhammad-Ali-and-his-successors-1805-82

facts.fact: Ottoman forces take Zabid in 1539 and Aden in 1538, making the Yemeni lowlands an Ottoman province until the Zaydi reconquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdali sultanate; https://www.britannica.com/place/Abdali-sultanate ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Taiz; https://www.britannica.com/place/Taiz

facts.fact: Ottoman armies occupy Sanaa in the 1540s and hold the northern Yemeni highlands until the Zaydi expulsion of 1635.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdali sultanate; https://www.britannica.com/place/Abdali-sultanate

facts.fact: The Abdali sultan of Lahej makes himself independent of the Zaydi imam around 1728 and takes Aden.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdali sultanate; https://www.britannica.com/place/Abdali-sultanate

facts.fact: Selim I receives the submission of the sharif of Mecca in 1517; Jeddah becomes the seat of an Ottoman governor and Red Sea garrison while the interior stays with the sharifs.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Marj Dabik; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Marj-Dabiq ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Arabia: Mamluk and Ottoman influence; https://www.britannica.com/place/history-of-Arabia-31558/Mamluk-and-Ottoman-influence

facts.fact: The Zaydi imams expel the Ottomans from the Yemeni highlands by 1635 and extend their rule over most of the southern highlands from Sanaa.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdali sultanate; https://www.britannica.com/place/Abdali-sultanate ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Taiz; https://www.britannica.com/place/Taiz

facts.fact: Ottoman campaigns of 1515-16 bring Diyarbakir and the Jazira under direct rule after the defeat of the Aq Qoyunlu and their local successors.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diyarbakir; https://www.britannica.com/place/Diyarbakir-Turkey

facts.fact: Suleyman I takes Baghdad in 1534 and Basra in 1546, organising southern Iraq as Ottoman provinces.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Iraq: the 16th-century conquest; https://www.britannica.com/place/Iraq/The-16th-century-conquest-of-Iraq-and-the-regime-imposed-by-Suleyman-I ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iraq iv: Safavid period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-iv-safavid-period/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I retakes Baghdad in 1623 and Safavid rule lasts until the Ottoman reconquest of 1638.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iraq iv: Safavid period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-iv-safavid-period/

facts.fact: Murad IV recaptures Baghdad in 1638; the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 fixes the Ottoman-Safavid frontier in Iraq.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Iraq: the 16th-century conquest; https://www.britannica.com/place/Iraq/The-16th-century-conquest-of-Iraq-and-the-regime-imposed-by-Suleyman-I ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Qasr-i Shirin; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Qasr-i-Shirin

facts.fact: The Jalayirid dynasty rules Iraq from Baghdad after losing Azerbaijan to Timur in 1386, until the Qara Qoyunlu take the city in 1410.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/

facts.fact: Hasan Kuchak of the Chobanids seizes Tabriz in 1338; Chobanid power ends with the death of Malek Ashraf in 1357 and the Jalayirids take Azerbaijan in 1359.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/chobanids-chupanids-pers/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/

facts.fact: The Muzaffarids take Isfahan in 1357; Timur sacks the city in 1387.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/mozaffarids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Isfahan vi: medieval period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/isfahan-vi-medieval-period/

facts.fact: Timur establishes his capital at Samarkand in 1370 and rules Transoxiana until the Shaybanid Uzbeks take Samarkand in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Timur conquers Khwarazm in 1379 and destroys Urgench in 1388; the region stays Timurid until the Uzbek conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Timur takes Herat in 1381 and ends the Kart dynasty in 1389; Herat becomes the Timurid capital under Shah Rukh and falls to the Shaybanids in 1507.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Al-e Kart; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/al-e-kart-or-perhaps-al-e-kort-an-east-iranian-dynasty-643-791-1245-1389/

facts.fact: Timur takes Nishapur and Tus in 1381 and Astarabad in 1384, absorbing the Sarbadar and Togha Timurid lands into his empire.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Togha Timur; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/togha-timur-ilkhan/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Al-e Kart; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/al-e-kart-or-perhaps-al-e-kort-an-east-iranian-dynasty-643-791-1245-1389/

facts.fact: Timur campaigns in Sistan and Kandahar in 1383; the region remains under Timurid princes until the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kandahar from the Mongol invasion through the Safavid era; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kandahar-from-the-mongol-invasion-through-the-safavid-era/

facts.fact: Timur subdues Mazandaran and Gilan in 1384-85, ending the local dynasties of the Caspian coast.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: The towns of Quhestan south of Khorasan pass under Timurid rule during the campaigns of 1381-93.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Al-e Kart; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/al-e-kart-or-perhaps-al-e-kort-an-east-iranian-dynasty-643-791-1245-1389/

facts.fact: Qara Yusuf takes Tabriz from the Timurids in 1406-08 and the Qara Qoyunlu rule Azerbaijan until Uzun Hasan destroys their power in 1467-68.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/

facts.fact: Baghdad passes to the Qara Qoyunlu in 1410-11 and stays in their hands until the Aq Qoyunlu take the city in 1469.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Timur takes Shiraz in 1393 and executes the last Muzaffarid princes; Timurid princes hold Fars until Jahan Shah takes it in 1452.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/mozaffarids/

facts.fact: Kerman passes to Timur with the fall of the Muzaffarids in 1393 and stays Timurid until the Qara Qoyunlu conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/mozaffarids/

facts.fact: Uzun Hasan moves the Aq Qoyunlu capital from Diyarbakir to Tabriz in 1468; Ismail I takes the city in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Baghdad passes to the Aq Qoyunlu in 1469 and is taken by Shah Ismail in 1508.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Shah Ismail takes Baghdad in 1508; the Ottomans take the city in 1534.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Ismail I takes Khorasan after the battle of Merv in 1510; Mashhad and western Khorasan remain Iranian through the Afghan and Afsharid periods.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/

facts.fact: The Baluch tribes of Makran acknowledge Safavid overlordship after the campaigns of the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I retakes Kandahar from the Mughals in 1622 and holds it until 1638.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kandahar from the Mongol invasion through the Safavid era; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kandahar-from-the-mongol-invasion-through-the-safavid-era/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas II recovers Kandahar in 1649; the Ghilzai revolt of 1709 ends Safavid rule in the city.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kandahar from the Mongol invasion through the Safavid era; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kandahar-from-the-mongol-invasion-through-the-safavid-era/

facts.fact: Ottoman troops occupy Yerevan and Nakhchivan in 1724 and keep them until the Persian reconquest of the 1730s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period (page 4); https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-4/

facts.fact: The Ottomans take Tbilisi in 1723 during the collapse of Safavid authority and hold it until 1735.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period (page 4); https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-4/

facts.fact: Tahmasp I moves the Safavid capital from Tabriz to Qazvin in 1548.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I moves the capital to Isfahan in 1598.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Nader Shah is crowned in 1736 and makes Mashhad the seat of his government.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Nader Shah; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nader-shah/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Afsharids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/afsharids-dynasty/

facts.fact: Karim Khan Zand rules from Shiraz from 1765 until his death in 1779.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Zand dynasty; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/zand-dynasty/

facts.fact: Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar establishes his capital at Tehran in 1786; the map location for Tehran is Rey.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period (page 4); https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-4/

facts.fact: After the Ottoman-Safavid war of 1578 the Samtskhe atabegate becomes an Ottoman eyalet centred on Akhaltsikhe, held until the Russian annexation of 1829.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Ottoman armies take Shirvan and Derbent in 1578 and hold the province until Shah Abbas I recovers it by 1607.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Khayr al-Din places Algiers under Ottoman suzerainty in 1519; the city becomes the seat of an Ottoman regency and passes to French rule in 1830.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Algiers; https://www.britannica.com/place/Algiers ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Barbarossa (Khayr al-Din); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Barbarossa

facts.fact: Khayr al-Din places Algiers under Ottoman suzerainty in 1519 and the regency extends over the central Maghreb until 1830.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Barbarossa (Khayr al-Din); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Barbarossa ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Algiers; https://www.britannica.com/place/Algiers

facts.fact: The eastern Algerian provinces around Constantine and Bejaia are brought under Ottoman rule in the sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Barbarossa (Khayr al-Din); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Barbarossa

facts.fact: The Ottoman regency of Algiers absorbs the Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen in the mid-sixteenth century, ending the Abd al-Wadid dynasty.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, North Africa: political fragmentation, c.1250-c.1500; https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Africa/Political-fragmentation-and-the-triumph-of-Islamic-culture-c-1250-c-1500 ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abd al-Wadid dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Abd-al-Wadid-dynasty

facts.fact: Spain takes Oran in 1509 and holds it, with its presidio at Mers el-Kebir, until 1708.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Oran; https://www.britannica.com/place/Oran

facts.fact: The Ottoman regency of Algiers recovers Oran in 1708 during the Spanish war of succession.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Oran; https://www.britannica.com/place/Oran

facts.fact: Spain retakes Oran in 1732 and holds it until the earthquake of 1790 and the evacuation of 1792.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Oran; https://www.britannica.com/place/Oran

facts.fact: Oran returns to Ottoman rule in 1792 after the Spanish evacuation.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Oran; https://www.britannica.com/place/Oran

facts.fact: French troops enter Oran in 1831.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Oran; https://www.britannica.com/place/Oran

facts.fact: The French army takes Algiers on 5 July 1830 and establishes colonial rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Algiers; https://www.britannica.com/place/Algiers

facts.fact: French forces capture Constantine in October 1837, completing the conquest of the eastern Algerian coast.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Constantine (Algeria); https://www.britannica.com/summary/Constantine-Algeria

facts.fact: Ottoman forces under Turgut Reis take Tripoli from the Knights of St John in 1551; the city becomes the seat of an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tripolitania; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tripolitania

facts.fact: Tripolitania is organised as an Ottoman province after 1551 and kept in the Ottoman orbit; the Karamanli family rules it as hereditary pashas from 1711 to 1835.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tripolitania; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tripolitania ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Libya: history; https://www.britannica.com/place/Libya/History

facts.fact: Spain takes Tripoli in 1510 and hands it to the Knights of St John in 1530.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tripolitania; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tripolitania

facts.fact: The Knights of St John hold Tripoli from 1530 until the Ottoman conquest of 1551.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tripolitania; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tripolitania

facts.fact: An Ottoman fleet under Uluc Ali takes Tunis in 1574, ending Hafsid rule; the Husaynid beys govern the province from 1705.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tunis; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tunis ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Husaynid dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Husaynid-dynasty

facts.fact: Portugal takes Ceuta in 1415 and keeps it after the Iberian Union; it passes to Spain by the Treaty of Lisbon in 1668.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ceuta; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ceuta ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Lisbon; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Lisbon

facts.fact: Spain holds Ceuta from 1668, when Portugal recognises Spanish possession, to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ceuta; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ceuta ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Lisbon; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Lisbon

facts.fact: Portugal takes Tangier in 1471 and cedes it to England with Catherine of Braganza in 1661-62.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Afonso V; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-V ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tangier; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tangier-Morocco

facts.fact: England holds Tangier from 1662 until the evacuation of 1684.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tangier; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tangier-Morocco

facts.fact: Morocco reoccupies Tangier after the English evacuation of 1684 and holds it to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tangier; https://www.britannica.com/place/Tangier-Morocco

facts.fact: Portugal takes Asilah in 1471 and holds it, with a Spanish garrison from 1578, until Morocco recovers it in 1589.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Afonso V; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-V ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Asilah; https://www.britannica.com/place/Asilah

facts.fact: Portugal takes Ksar es-Seghir (Alcacer Ceguer) in 1458 and abandons it in 1550.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Afonso V; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-V

facts.fact: Portugal holds Safi on the Atlantic coast from 1508 to 1541.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Safi; https://www.britannica.com/place/Safi

facts.fact: Portugal takes Azemmour in 1513 and loses it to the Saadians in 1541.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Safi; https://www.britannica.com/place/Safi

facts.fact: Portugal holds Agadir (Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gue) from 1505 to 1541.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Agadir; https://www.britannica.com/place/Agadir-Morocco

facts.fact: Portugal fortifies Mazagan (El Jadida) in the early sixteenth century and holds the fortress until 1769.
facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Portuguese City of Mazagan (El Jadida); https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1058/

facts.fact: Spain holds Larache on the Atlantic coast from 1610 to 1689.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Larache; https://www.britannica.com/place/Larache

facts.fact: Spain occupies Melilla in 1497 and holds the presidio to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Melilla; https://www.britannica.com/place/Melilla

facts.fact: Spain occupies La Mamora (Mehdia) from 1614 until Morocco recovers it in 1681.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Larache; https://www.britannica.com/place/Larache

facts.fact: The Saadians take Marrakesh in 1525 and rule from the city until the Alaouite takeover of 1666.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sadi dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sadi-dynasty

facts.fact: The Alaouites take Fez in 1666 and make it their capital.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, al-Rashid (Alaouite sultan); https://www.britannica.com/biography/al-Rashid

facts.fact: Moulay Ismail makes Meknes the Moroccan capital in 1673.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Meknes; https://www.britannica.com/place/Meknes

facts.fact: After the death of Moulay Ismail in 1727 the court returns to Marrakesh.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Meknes; https://www.britannica.com/place/Meknes

facts.fact: Qara Yusuf takes Tabriz from the Timurids and founds the Qara Qoyunlu state, destroyed by the Aq Qoyunlu in 1467-68.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/

facts.fact: Uzun Hasan destroys the Qara Qoyunlu, moves his capital from Diyarbakir to Tabriz and rules Iran until the Safavid conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Ismail I decrees Twelver Shiism the official religion of the Safavid state after taking Tabriz in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Albuquerque attacks Hormuz in 1507 and establishes Portuguese rule with a fortress in 1515; the Portuguese hold the island and Bandar Abbas until 1622.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: An Anglo-Persian expedition takes Qeshm and Hormuz in 1622, ending Portuguese control of the strait.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: Muhammad ibn Saud and the Wahhabi preacher establish the Saudi emirate at Diriyah in 1744 and rule central Najd from it.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudi Arabia: history; https://www.britannica.com/place/Saudi-Arabia/History

facts.fact: Saudi forces take al-Hasa from the Banu Khalid in the early 1790s, extending the Diriyah emirate to the Gulf coast.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudi Arabia: history; https://www.britannica.com/place/Saudi-Arabia/History

facts.fact: Saudi forces occupy Mecca in 1803 and hold the holy cities until the Egyptian reconquest of 1812-13.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Saudi Arabia: history; https://www.britannica.com/place/Saudi-Arabia/History

facts.fact: An Egyptian army under Tusun Pasha recovers Mecca and Medina for the Ottomans in 1812-13; Egyptian troops garrison the Hejaz until 1840.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Egypt: Muhammad Ali and his successors; https://www.britannica.com/place/Egypt/Muhammad-Ali-and-his-successors-1805-82

facts.fact: Egyptian forces recover Medina in 1812-13 and remain responsible for the Hejaz garrisons until 1840.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Egypt: Muhammad Ali and his successors; https://www.britannica.com/place/Egypt/Muhammad-Ali-and-his-successors-1805-82

facts.fact: Portugal occupies Muscat from the second decade of the sixteenth century until the Omanis retake the city in 1650.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Oman; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/oman/

facts.fact: The Ya'rubid imam Sultan b. Sayf expels the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650 and the city becomes the seat of Omani power.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Oman; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/oman/

facts.fact: Nasir b. Murshid is elected imam at Rustaq in 1624 and the Ya'rubid imamate unifies the Omani interior and coast; the Al Bu Said take over in the 1740s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Oman; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/oman/

facts.fact: Venice rules Crete as its overseas colony until the Ottoman conquest of Candia in 1669.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Venice takes direct control of Negroponte from its triarchs at the end of the fourteenth century and holds Euboea until 1470.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: The Genoese trading colony of Amasra on the Black Sea coast is held until the Ottoman annexation of 1461.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Candar dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Candar-dynasty

facts.fact: The Genoese family of the Gattilusio and the Maona of Phocaea hold the alum works of Old and New Phocaea until the Ottoman takeover in 1455.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Candar dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Candar-dynasty

facts.fact: Muhammad Shaybani takes Samarkand in 1501 and the Uzbek Shaybanid dynasty rules Transoxiana from Bukhara, succeeded by the Janid and Manghit dynasties.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bukhara iv; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iv/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/

facts.fact: The Arabshahid branch of the Shaybanids establishes an independent khanate in Khwarazm in 1511, ruled from Urgench and later Khiva.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bukhara iv; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iv/

facts.fact: Shahrukh Biy founds an independent principality in the Fergana valley in 1709, which becomes the khanate of Kokand and takes Tashkent in 1809.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kokand khanate; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kokand-khanate/

facts.fact: The Shaybanid Uzbeks take Samarkand in 1501 and rule Transoxiana from Bukhara for the rest of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bukhara iv; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iv/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/

facts.fact: Badakhshan and the upper Oxus principalities come under Bukharan rule in the sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bukhara iv; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iv/

facts.fact: The Kokand khanate emerges in the Fergana valley in 1709 and expands over the surrounding towns in the eighteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kokand khanate; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kokand-khanate/

facts.fact: Timurid rule extends over the northern Transoxianan towns of Khujand and Jizzakh after 1370.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: The Ottoman eyalet of Cildir is established at Akhaltsikhe after the 1578 campaign and held until the Russian annexation of 1829.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of the Bulgarian Tsardom in 1393 brings the northern Thracian districts under direct Ottoman rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bulgaria: the second Bulgarian empire; https://www.britannica.com/place/Bulgaria/The-second-Bulgarian-empire

facts.fact: Venetian forces under Francesco Morosini complete the conquest of the Peloponnese in 1687; the conquest is confirmed at Karlowitz in 1699.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Carlowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Carlowitz ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: The Muzaffarids take Shiraz in 1353 and rule Fars until Timur destroys the dynasty in 1393.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/mozaffarids/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I takes the port of Gamrun (Bandar Abbas) from Hormuz and develops it as the Persian Gulf outlet.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: The Ottoman conquest of Crete is completed with the surrender of Candia in 1669; the island remains Ottoman past the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Venetian-Turkish wars; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Venetian-Turkish-wars

facts.fact: Preveza returns to Ottoman rule after the Venetian war and stays Ottoman past the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz

facts.fact: Vonitsa returns to Ottoman rule after the Venetian war and stays Ottoman past the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz

facts.fact: The Ottoman province of Lahsa is established in al-Hasa after the conquest of the district, lasting until the Banu Khalid expel the Ottomans around 1670.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Arabia: Mamluk and Ottoman influence; https://www.britannica.com/place/history-of-Arabia-31558/Mamluk-and-Ottoman-influence

facts.fact: The Banu Khalid expel the Ottomans in 1670 and rule al-Hasa independently until the Saudi conquest in the 1790s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Arabia: Mamluk and Ottoman influence; https://www.britannica.com/place/history-of-Arabia-31558/Mamluk-and-Ottoman-influence

facts.fact: The Banu Khalid emirate centred on al-Ahsa controls the Qatif oasis after the Ottoman withdrawal.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Arabia: Mamluk and Ottoman influence; https://www.britannica.com/place/history-of-Arabia-31558/Mamluk-and-Ottoman-influence

facts.fact: Portugal holds Bahrain from the 1510s until the Safavid reconquest of 1602.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: Safavid forces take Bahrain from the Portuguese in 1602 and hold the islands until the Omani occupation of 1717.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: The Ottomans reconquer the Morea from Venice in 1715; Venetian claims are surrendered at Passarowitz in 1718.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Passarowitz; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Passarowitz ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Timur takes Isfahan in 1387 and the Jibal towns in the 1390s; the region stays Timurid until Jahan Shah takes it in 1452.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Isfahan vi: medieval period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/isfahan-vi-medieval-period/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Jahan Shah extends Qara Qoyunlu rule over Iraq-i Ajam, Fars and Kerman in 1452-53, taking them from the Timurid princes.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Uzun Hasan makes Tabriz his capital in 1468 and the Aq Qoyunlu hold central and southern Iran until the Safavid conquest of 1503.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Safavid armies take Fars, Kerman and Iraq-i Ajam in 1503; the region remains part of the Iranian state through the Afsharid, Zand and Qajar periods.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Timur takes Tabriz in 1386 and breaks Jalayirid power in Azerbaijan, which passes to the Qara Qoyunlu after his death.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: Ismail I takes Tabriz in 1501 and rules from the city until Tahmasp moves the capital to Qazvin in 1548.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Azerbaijan remains the core Safavid province after the capital moves to Qazvin, and stays Iranian through the successor dynasties.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Quhestan and the eastern Iranian towns pass to the Safavids with the conquests of 1503 and remain Iranian to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Khuzestan and the Kurdish districts of Luristan and Kermanshah are absorbed into the Safavid state in the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Ottoman armies occupy Hamadan and Kermanshah during the Afghan crisis and hold them until Nader Shah expels them in the 1730s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period (page 4); https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-4/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Nader Shah; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nader-shah/

facts.fact: The Crnojevic lordship of Zeta submits to the Ottomans at the end of the fifteenth century; the province is administered as the sanjak of Montenegro.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Serbia: conquest by the Ottoman Turks; https://www.britannica.com/place/Serbia/Conquest-by-the-Ottoman-Turks

facts.fact: Selim I takes Erzurum and Bayburt after the battle of Chaldiran in 1514 and they become the core of an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Suleyman I takes Van from the Safavids in 1548 and organises the Lake Van basin as an Ottoman province.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Kars passes under Ottoman control during the sixteenth-century wars with the Safavids and remains an Ottoman fortress town.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: The Kurdish and Arab principalities of Mardin and Hasankeyf are absorbed into the Ottoman province of Diyarbakir in the sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diyarbakir; https://www.britannica.com/place/Diyarbakir-Turkey

facts.fact: Ismail I takes Herat in 1510 and eastern Khorasan stays Safavid until the Abdali Afghan revolt takes Herat in 1716.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/

facts.fact: Nader Shah recovers Herat from the Abdali Afghans in 1729 and holds it until his death, after which it passes to the Durrani state.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat iii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/herat-iii/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Nader Shah; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nader-shah/

facts.fact: The Caspian provinces of Gilan, Mazandaran and Astarabad are brought under Safavid control in the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Sistan is disputed between the Safavids and the local Mihrabanid and Baluch rulers; Iranian control is asserted in the sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kandahar from the Mongol invasion through the Safavid era; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kandahar-from-the-mongol-invasion-through-the-safavid-era/

facts.fact: The Ottomans seize Gallipoli in 1354 after an earthquake wrecks its walls, gaining their first permanent base in Europe.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Orhan (Ottoman sultan); https://www.britannica.com/biography/Orhan ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: With the conquest of Thrace after 1366 the Ottomans take the whole of the Gallipoli peninsula and its hinterland.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of the Maritsa River; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Maritsa-River

facts.fact: Murad I takes Adrianople and renames it Edirne; it becomes the Ottoman capital before Constantinople.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Murad I; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Murad-I ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Edirne; https://www.britannica.com/place/Edirne

facts.fact: The Thracian hinterland of Edirne is brought under Ottoman rule in the later fourteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of the Maritsa River; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Maritsa-River

facts.fact: Mehmed II captures Constantinople on 29 May 1453; the city becomes the Ottoman capital.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: The fall of Constantinople in 1453 brings the whole of its province, including Silivri and Catalca, under Ottoman rule.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ottoman Empire: Osman and Orhan; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ottoman-Empire/Osman-and-Orhan

facts.fact: Orhan completes the annexation of the Karesi lands around Bursa, absorbing the remaining coastal districts.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Karasi dynasty; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Karasi-dynasty

facts.fact: The Khiva khanate controls Khwarazm and its oasis towns from 1511 onward.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bukhara iv; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iv/

facts.fact: The northern Hejaz districts held by the Mamluks pass to the Ottomans with the conquest of Egypt in 1517 and are administered from Jeddah and Medina.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Marj Dabik; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Marj-Dabiq ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, History of Arabia: Mamluk and Ottoman influence; https://www.britannica.com/place/history-of-Arabia-31558/Mamluk-and-Ottoman-influence

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I recovers Shirvan and Derbent from the Ottomans by 1607 and the province stays Safavid until the Russian and Ottoman invasions of the 1720s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: The Armenian highlands around Yerevan and Nakhchivan are absorbed into the Safavid state in the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: The Mamluks conquer the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia in 1375 and hold its towns until the Ottoman conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Little Armenia; https://www.britannica.com/place/Little-Armenia ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cilicia; https://www.britannica.com/place/Cilicia

facts.fact: Selim I takes the Cilician towns from the Mamluks in 1516; they pass to direct Ottoman administration with the end of the Ramazanoglu principality.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Marj Dabik; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Marj-Dabiq

facts.fact: The Aq Qoyunlu hold the Karabakh and Mughan plains east of Armenia until the Safavid conquest.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/
