facts.fact: The Safavids take Ganja and the Mughan plain in the early sixteenth century and keep them until the Russian annexations of the nineteenth century.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: The Ottoman campaigns of 1514-17 bring the Kurdish and Turkmen emirates of eastern Anatolia into the empire as provinces and tributary sanjaks.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/ ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diyarbakir; https://www.britannica.com/place/Diyarbakir-Turkey

facts.fact: The French take over the Ionian Islands when Venice falls in 1797 and hold them until the British occupation.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Britain occupies the Ionian Islands from 1809 and holds them as a protectorate from 1815; they are ceded to Greece in 1864.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Kythera passes to France with the other Venetian possessions in 1797.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Britain takes Kythera with the Ionian Islands in 1809 and keeps it as part of the protectorate.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ionian Islands; https://www.britannica.com/place/Ionian-Islands

facts.fact: Venice acquires Argos and Nauplia in 1388 and holds the Argolid ports until the Ottoman conquest of 1540.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: Suleyman I takes Nauplia and Argos from Venice in 1540 with Monemvasia.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Despotate of Morea; https://www.britannica.com/place/Despotate-of-Morea

facts.fact: The Jalayirids rule Azerbaijan from Tabriz until Timur takes the city in 1386.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Jalayerids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids/

facts.fact: Shah Abbas I recovers Ganja and the Mughan plain from the Ottomans by 1607; they stay Iranian until the Russian annexations.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/safavids/

facts.fact: Uzun Hasan moves the Aq Qoyunlu capital from Diyarbakir to Tabriz in 1468; the city stays theirs until Ismail I takes it in 1501.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu confederation; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/aq-qoyunlu-confederation/

facts.fact: The Fergana valley is held by local Chagatai begs after the collapse of Timurid power and before the rise of Kokand in 1709.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kokand khanate; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kokand-khanate/

facts.fact: The Ottomans take Tabriz in 1585 and hold it until Shah Abbas I recovers the city in 1603.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Iran ii2: Islamic period; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-ii2-islamic-period-page-3/

facts.fact: Omani forces take Bahrain from the Safavids in 1717 and hold the islands until the Persian reconquest of the 1730s.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Oman; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/oman/ ; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: Nader Shah brings Bahrain back under Persian control in the 1730s; the Persians hold the islands until 1783.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: The Al Khalifa branch of the Utub captures Bahrain from the Persians in 1783 and rules the islands from Manama.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: The Al Khalifa rule Bahrain from Manama after their conquest of 1783.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hormuz ii; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hormuz-ii/

facts.fact: Austria takes over the Bocche di Cattaro and Dalmatia when Venice falls in 1797 and holds them, apart from a short French occupation, past the end of the timeline.
facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kotor; https://www.britannica.com/place/Kotor ; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Dalmatia; https://www.britannica.com/place/Dalmatia

Tatars entry, Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (CIUS, University of Alberta): the Golden Horde disintegrated in the early 15th century and independent khanates, including the Kazan Khanate, emerged; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CA%5CTatars.htm. Conquest of Kazan by Ivan the Terrible in 1552: UNESCO WHC, Historic and Architectural Complex of the Kazan Kremlin; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/980/
facts.fact: Kazan Khanate established on the middle Volga out of the disintegrating Golden Horde, centred on Kazan; conquered by Muscovy in 1552.

facts.source: Kazan Khanate as successor of the Golden Horde on the middle Volga: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Tatars; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CA%5CTatars.htm and Golden Horde; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/golden-horde
facts.fact: Kazan Khanate holds the Kazan and Bolghar areas of the middle Volga, taken from the Golden Horde.

facts.source: UNESCO WHC 980, Kazan Kremlin: 'It was conquered by Ivan the Terrible in 1552'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/980/
facts.fact: Muscovy annexes the Kazan Khanate after the capture of Kazan in 1552.

facts.source: B. Spuler, 'Astrakhan', Encyclopaedia Iranica II/8: 'In 1466, with the decline of the Golden Horde, Astrakhan became the capital of an independent Tatar khanate'; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/astrakhan
facts.fact: Astrakhan Khanate becomes independent on the lower Volga with its capital at Astrakhan as the Golden Horde declines.

facts.source: B. Spuler, 'Astrakhan', Encyclopaedia Iranica: independent Tatar khanate from 1466, falling to Russia 'first in 1554 and finally in 1556-57'; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/astrakhan
facts.fact: Astrakhan Khanate holds the lower Volga delta around Astrakhan.

facts.source: B. Spuler, 'Astrakhan', Encyclopaedia Iranica: the khanate 'fell into Russian hands, first in 1554 and finally in 1556-57'; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/astrakhan
facts.fact: Muscovy takes the Astrakhan Khanate; the lower Volga passes to Russian rule.

facts.source: Entries 'Crimea' and 'Crimean Khanate', Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine: formation 'in the Crimea in 1449 of a separate state known as the Crimean Khanate, under the leadership of the Girei dynasty, which held power until 1783'; first capital Solkhat/Kirim; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimeanKhanate.htm
facts.fact: Crimean Khanate is established under the Girei dynasty, first at Solkhat (Staryi Krym), with Ottoman supremacy recognised from 1478.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Crimea: the khanate formed in 1449 and held power until 1783; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm
facts.fact: Crimean Khanate holds the Crimean peninsula, apart from the Genoese and Theodoro enclaves on the south coast.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Crimea: 'Besides the Crimea the khanate controlled the lower Dnipro River, the steppes along the coast of the Sea of Azov'; the Great Horde's final collapse c. 1502 (Encyclopaedia Iranica, Golden Horde; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/golden-horde) opens the north Black Sea steppe to the khanate; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm
facts.fact: Crimean Khanate extends its authority over the lower Dnipro steppe north of the peninsula after the Great Horde collapses.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Crimea and Turkey: Crimean authority over the north Black Sea steppe until Russia acquired the land between the Boh and Dnister by the Treaty of Iaşi in 1791; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CU%5CTurkey.htm
facts.fact: Crimean Khanate holds the steppe between the Boh and the Dnister (Yedisan) until Russia takes it in 1791.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Crimea: khanate controlled 'the steppes along the coast of the Sea of Azov'; annexed with the Crimea in 1783; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm
facts.fact: Crimean Khanate holds the steppe along the northern shore of the Sea of Azov.

facts.source: UNESCO WHC 1170, Yaroslavl: 'The city of Yaroslavl started developing in 1463 when Yaroslavl Principality [was annexed]'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1170/; Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: Muscovy annexed Yaroslavl (1463); https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy annexes the principality of Yaroslavl under Ivan III.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: Muscovy annexed the principalities of Yaroslavl (1463), Rostov (1474), and Tver (1485); https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy annexes the principality of Rostov.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Novgorod the Great: Ivan III 'annexed much of the republic's territory in 1471 and then forced the city ... to recognize Moscow's suzerainty in 1478'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CN%5CO%5CNovgorodtheGreat.htm; Russia: Novgorod the Great (1471-89); https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy absorbs the Novgorod republic, its northern and eastern districts and the Karelian and Pomor lands, after the submission of 1478.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: Muscovy annexed Tver in 1485; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy annexes the principality of Tver, ending the last great rival of Moscow in the upper Volga.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: Ivan III annexed 'the Viatka territory (1489)'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy annexes the Vyatka lands beyond the Volga.

facts.source: Inferred from the general account of Muscovite expansion: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: the Muscovite principality 'expanded by conquest and purchase until it acquired all the other former principalities of Kyivan Rus''; no page consulted dates the Nizhnii Novgorod annexation; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy takes over the Nizhnii Novgorod, Gorodets and Galich lands on the middle Volga (inferred date 1392).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: Ivan III annexed 'the greater part of the principality of Ryazan', without a date; the final absorption is dated here by inference to 1521; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy absorbs the principality of Ryazan (inferred).

facts.source: Inferred: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia records the annexation of Pskov within the consolidation under Ivan III and Vasilii III without giving a year; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy ends the independence of Pskov (inferred 1510).

facts.source: Inferred: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia records Muscovite war with Lithuania over the lands of Rus' from 1487-1537 without dating the capture of Smolensk; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy takes Smolensk and its district from Lithuania (inferred 1514); it holds them until 1611.

facts.source: Inferred: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: the Commonwealth intervened during the Time of Troubles and 'Poland renewed hostilities in 1617 and won back Starodub and Novhorod-Siverskyi' at the Armistice of Deulino (1618), implying the loss of the western borderlands; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth holds Smolensk and its district after the Time of Troubles (inferred 1611).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: war with the Commonwealth from 1654; the territorial settlement confirmed at Andrusovo (1667); https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CA%5CN%5CAndrusovoTreatyof.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy recovers Smolensk and its district in the war of 1654.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: 'In the course of those conflicts Muscovy managed to incorporate the Ukrainian principalities of Starodub and Novhorod-Siverskyi (1503-17)'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy incorporates the Siverian lands of Starodub and Novhorod-Siverskyi during its wars with Lithuania.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: 'Poland renewed hostilities in 1617 and won back Starodub and Novhorod-Siverskyi (according to the Armistice of Deulino in 1618)'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: The Commonwealth wins back the Siverian lands at the Armistice of Deulino.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia and Andrusovo, Treaty of: war from 1654 and the settlement of 1667 assigning the left bank, including Chernihiv and Starodub, to Muscovy; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CA%5CN%5CAndrusovoTreatyof.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy takes the Siverian lands again in the war of 1654, confirmed at Andrusovo.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Andrusovo, Treaty of (13 January 1667): 'Left-Bank Ukraine remained under Muscovite rule, while Right-Bank Ukraine was transferred to Poland'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CA%5CN%5CAndrusovoTreatyof.htm; Eternal Peace of 1686; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CE%5CT%5CEternalPeaceof1686.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy keeps Left-Bank Ukraine under the Truce of Andrusovo, confirmed by the Eternal Peace of 1686.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Eternal Peace of 1686: 'Left-Bank Ukraine with Kyiv (for a compensation of 146,000 rubles) ... were to come under Russian control'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CE%5CT%5CEternalPeaceof1686.htm; Kyiv entry; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CK%5CY%5CKyiv.htm
facts.fact: Kyiv stays with Muscovy and its possession is formalised in the Eternal Peace of 1686.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Right-Bank Ukraine: annexed by the Russian Empire in the partitions of Poland, the third of 1795 completing the process; Poland entry: Russia acquired all of Poland's Ukrainian possessions in 1772, 1793 and 1795; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CI%5CRight6BankUkraine.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes Right-Bank Ukraine in the second and third partitions of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland and Right-Bank Ukraine: the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795 gave Russia all of Poland's Ukrainian lands except Galicia and Bukovyna; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CI%5CRight6BankUkraine.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes Podolia from Poland in the second partition.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: Russia acquired all of Poland's Ukrainian possessions other than Galicia and Bukovyna in the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes eastern Volhynia in the third partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Belarus: 'After the partitions of Poland in 1772-95 all Belarusian territories were annexed by Russia'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CB%5CE%5CBelarus.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes the eastern Belarusian lands (Polatsk, Vitsebsk, Mstsislaw) in the first partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Belarus: all Belarusian territories annexed by Russia in the partitions of 1772-95; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CB%5CE%5CBelarus.htm; Poland; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes central and western Belarus in the second partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: the Polish state existed until 1795 and was partitioned in 1772, 1793 and 1795; Lithuania entry on the Grand Duchy within the Commonwealth; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CL%5CI%5CLithuania.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes Lithuania proper and Samogitia in the third partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Belarus: all Belarusian territories annexed by Russia in the partitions of 1772-95; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CB%5CE%5CBelarus.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes Polesia in the third partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: Russia acquired all of Poland's Ukrainian possessions 'other than Galicia and Bukovyna (which were annexed by the Austrian Empire)' in the partitioning of Poland (1772, 1793, and 1795); https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: The Habsburg monarchy annexes Red Ruthenia (Galicia) in the first partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: the partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, and 1795) divided the Commonwealth between Russia, Prussia and Austria; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Prussia annexes Greater Poland in the second partition of Poland.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Congress Kingdom of Poland: 'Semiautonomous state established by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 out of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw and tied to the Russian Empire by a political and dynastic union (the Russian tsar was also the king of Poland)'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CO%5CCongressKingdomofPoland.htm
facts.fact: The Congress Kingdom of Poland is created at Vienna and united with Russia by a dynastic union, so its territory passes to the Russian crown.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795 divided the Commonwealth between Russia, Prussia and Austria; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Austria takes Lesser Poland with Krakow in the third partition of Poland, holding it until the war of 1809.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Turkey: 'In 1774 the triangle between the Dnipro River and the Boh River was wrested from Turkish control, and the Crimean Khanate was made independent of Turkey (under the Peace Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca)'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CU%5CTurkey.htm
facts.fact: Russia takes the steppe between the Dnipro and the Boh from the Crimean Khanate under the Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Turkey: 'in 1791 (under the Treaty of Iasi) it acquired the territory between the lower Boh River and the Dnister River'; Ochakiv entry confirms Russian acquisition in 1791; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CU%5CTurkey.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CO%5CC%5COchakiv.htm
facts.fact: Russia takes the land between the lower Boh and the Dnister (Yedisan, with Ochakiv) under the Treaty of Iasi.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Crimea: Russia's protection from 1774 and 'finally occupied it in 1783'; Turkey: 'In 1783 Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CC%5CR%5CCrimea.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CT%5CU%5CTurkey.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes the Crimean Khanate, ending Tatar rule in the peninsula and on the Azov steppe.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Bessarabia: 'After Russia annexed Bessarabia in 1812, the population of Bessarabia increased rapidly'; Russia entry: 'In 1812 Russia acquired Bessarabia'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CB%5CE%5CBessarabia.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes Bessarabia (the lands between the Dnister and the Prut) under the Treaty of Bucharest.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Saint Petersburg: 'From 1712 to 1918 it was the capital of the Russian Empire'; Moscow entry: 'From 1478 to 1712 Moscow was the center of the unified state of Muscovy'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CS%5CA%5CSaintPetersburg.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CM%5CO%5CMoscow.htm
facts.fact: Peter I moves the seat of government from Moscow to the new city on the Neva, which remains the imperial capital.

facts.source: Inferred from Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Siberia: Russian traders and state servitors 'colonized Siberia and the Far East in the 17th and 18th centuries'; the article gives no conquest dates; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CS%5CI%5CSiberia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy extends direct rule over western Siberia after the defeat of the Khanate of Sibir (inferred, 1586-1604).

facts.source: Inferred from Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Siberia: Russian traders and state servitors colonized Siberia and the Far East in the 17th and 18th centuries, reaching Kamchatka; the article gives no military dates. Applied to a region with no polity in 1337; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CS%5CI%5CSiberia.htm
facts.fact: Muscovy extends direct rule across eastern Siberia to the Pacific, first over unorganised hunting and reindeer-herding communities (inferred, 1632-1650).

facts.source: Inferred: no institutional page consulted covers the Kazakh steppe; the Russian administrative reorganisation of the Junior and Middle Hordes in the 1820s is the point at which direct rule is conventionally dated; background on the steppe's earlier Tatar rulers in Encyclopaedia Iranica, Golden Horde; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/golden-horde
facts.fact: Russia imposes direct administration on the Kazakh steppe of the former Golden Horde (inferred, 1822-1824).

facts.source: Inferred: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia records Russian expansion down the Volga after the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan without dating the Bashkir submission; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia extends direct rule over Bashkiria after the fall of Kazan and Astrakhan (inferred).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: 'In the 19th century it acquired Finland, Bessarabia, and much of Poland'; no year or treaty is given in the source consulted; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia takes Finland from Sweden and keeps it as an autonomous grand duchy (inferred, war of 1808-1809).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: 'In the 19th century it acquired Finland, Bessarabia, and much of Poland as well as Subcaucasia and more of Asia'; no dates are given in the source consulted; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia absorbs the Georgian kingdom and the neighbouring south Caucasian lands (inferred, 1801-1828).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Bakhchysarai: 'Bakhchysarai was established as the Crimean Tatar capital in 1532'; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CB%5CA%5CBakhchysarai.htm
facts.fact: The Crimean khan moves his seat from Solkhat to Bakhchysarai, which remains the khanate's capital until 1783.

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Russia: in the 18th century the state 'expanded to the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea by acquiring Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Belarus'; no treaty year given in the source consulted; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia acquires the Baltic provinces of Estonia and Livonia (with Osel) from Sweden and the Livonian Order's successor estates (inferred, conquest 1710, ceded 1721).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Poland: the Commonwealth was partitioned in 1772, 1793 and 1795, Russia taking the largest share; the Duchy of Courland was a Polish fief until the third partition; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CP%5CO%5CPoland.htm
facts.fact: Russia annexes the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia in the third partition of Poland (inferred).

facts.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, Saint Petersburg: the city was founded in 1703 in the Neva delta on land taken from Sweden, and the empire acquired Estonia and Latvia in the 18th century; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CS%5CA%5CSaintPetersburg.htm ; https://www.encyclopediaofukraine.com/display.asp?linkpath=pages%5CR%5CU%5CRussia.htm
facts.fact: Russia takes Ingria at the mouth of the Neva, where Saint Petersburg is founded in 1703 (ceded by Sweden in 1721).

facts.source: M. P. Pedani, 'Venetian Consuls in Egypt and Syria in the Ottoman Age' (2006), pp. 7-21; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/Venetian-Consuls-in-Egypt-MP-Pedani.pdf; 'From Constantinople to Istanbul: The Residences of the Venetian Bailo (13th-16th c.)', European Journal of Archaeology; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-journal-of-archaeology/article/abs/from-constantinople-to-istanbul-the-residences-of-the-venetian-bailo-thirteenth-to-sixteenth-centuries/A3A93DE611C7703416165A2C39763465
facts.fact: Venetian bailo and the Venetian merchant quarter at Constantinople, an office held continuously from 1265/1268 and confirmed by the 1454 agreement with Mehmed II, which gave the bailo civil jurisdiction over Venetians in the empire; it lasted until the Republic fell in 1797.

facts.source: M. P. Pedani, 'Venetian Consuls in Egypt and Syria in the Ottoman Age' (2006), pp. 7-21; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/Venetian-Consuls-in-Egypt-MP-Pedani.pdf; A. Rizzo, 'Travelling and Trading through Mamluk Territory' (2021); https://www.academia.edu/48880767/
facts.fact: Venetian consul and fondaco community at Alexandria, present through the Mamluk period and kept after the Ottoman conquest, with consuls drawn from the nobility after 1586 and resident until the end of the Republic; consular presence was interrupted by war years.

facts.source: M. P. Pedani, 'Venetian Consuls in Egypt and Syria in the Ottoman Age' (2006), pp. 7-21; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/Venetian-Consuls-in-Egypt-MP-Pedani.pdf; 'The Importance of the Role of the Venetian Baili', Acta Orientalia 75/1 (2022), citing Mola 2000: 57 on the 1545 and 1548 transfers; https://www.akjournals.com/view/journals/062/75/1/article-p79.pdf
facts.fact: Venetian consul in Mamluk Damascus; the sultan began paying the consul a salary in 1422, and the consulate was closed in 1545 when it was moved to Tripoli in Syria.

facts.source: 'The Importance of the Role of the Venetian Baili', Acta Orientalia 75/1 (2022), citing Mola 2000: 57 on the 1545 and 1548 transfers; https://www.akjournals.com/view/journals/062/75/1/article-p79.pdf; M. P. Pedani, 'Venetian Consuls in Egypt and Syria in the Ottoman Age' (2006), pp. 7-21; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/Venetian-Consuls-in-Egypt-MP-Pedani.pdf
facts.fact: Venetian consulate transferred to Aleppo in 1548, where 250 Venetian merchants were recorded in 1559 and the consul was thereafter chosen from the nobility; it remained the senior Venetian consulate in Syria until 1797.

facts.source: 'On the Knowledge of Persia in the Republic of Venice', Austrian Academy of Sciences, section 7 (Venetian baili at Trebizond, 1319 treaty, list 1320-1454); https://www.austriaca.at/0xc1aa5576%200x0022a601.pdf
facts.fact: Venetian colony at Trebizond headed by a bailo under the privileges granted by Alexios II in 1319, with a baili list running 1320-1454 and galleys calling until 1452; ended with the Ottoman conquest of the city in 1461.

facts.source: S. P. Karpov, reviewed in Byzantinische Zeitschrift/ByzRev 06.2024.031 (Venetian and Genoese quarters and consuls at Tana, 1333-1336 caravanserai, 1347 yarlyk, end 1475); https://ejournals.uni-muenster.de/byzrev/article/download/5634/5746/16035
facts.fact: Venetian quarter and consul at Tana on the Don, with a caravanserai built in 1333-1336 under a khan's concession and a separate quarter confirmed by the 1347 yarlyk; the settlement held out until the Ottoman conquest of 1475.

facts.source: 'The Genoese Levantine Colonies at the Birth of Ottoman Imperial Rule' (Pera/Galata, Trebizond, Caffa, Chios); https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/The-Genoese-Levantine-colonies.pdf
facts.fact: Genoese colony of Pera/Galata across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, an administered settlement with its own podesta and notarial archive that concluded its own agreement with Bayezid I in 1389; the colonial regime ended with the Ottoman conquest of 1453. Caffa and Chios were Genoese-ruled territory, not residencies, and belong to the ownership groups.

facts.source: S. P. Karpov, reviewed in Byzantinische Zeitschrift/ByzRev 06.2024.031 (Venetian and Genoese quarters and consuls at Tana, 1333-1336 caravanserai, 1347 yarlyk, end 1475); https://ejournals.uni-muenster.de/byzrev/article/download/5634/5746/16035; 'The Genoese Levantine Colonies at the Birth of Ottoman Imperial Rule' (Pera/Galata, Trebizond, Caffa, Chios); https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/The-Genoese-Levantine-colonies.pdf
facts.fact: Genoese quarter and consul at Tana beside the Venetian one, under the khan's authority, ending with the Ottoman conquest in 1475.

facts.source: 'The Genoese Levantine Colonies at the Birth of Ottoman Imperial Rule' (Pera/Galata, Trebizond, Caffa, Chios); https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/The-Genoese-Levantine-colonies.pdf; 'Empire of Trebizond'; https://www.worldhistory.org/Empire_of_Trebizond/
facts.fact: Genoese colony at Trebizond around the Leonkastron fort bought in 1306, with a consul appointed from Genoa and a position comparable to Galata's; ended with the Ottoman conquest of 1461.

facts.source: A. Rizzo, 'A Survey of Florentine-Mamluk Relations', Mamluk Studies Review XXIV; https://orbi.uliege.be/bitstream/2268/267965/1/MSR-XXIV-Rizzo%20(published%20version).pdf
facts.fact: Florentine consulate at Alexandria opened by the 1422 embassy to Sultan Barsbay, with Ugolino Rondinelli, Antonio Minerbetti and then Francesco Manelli (1425-1434) as consuls and later appointees close to the Medici; the end date is inferred from the collapse of the Mamluk regime and the reordering of privileges after 1517.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf; 'The strange death of the Levant Company', History Today/Historia; https://historiamag.com/strange-death-of-levant-company/; Oxford Reference, Levant Company; https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100102153
facts.fact: English embassy and Levant Company factory at Constantinople from William Harborne's appointment in 1583; the ambassador doubled as the company's senior consul until 1804, and the establishment passed to the Crown when the company was dissolved in 1825.

facts.source: 'The Genoese Levantine Colonies at the Birth of Ottoman Imperial Rule' (Pera/Galata, Trebizond, Caffa, Chios); https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/The-Genoese-Levantine-colonies.pdf; L. Mitler, 'The Genoese in Galata: 1453-1682', International Journal of Middle East Studies, cited there
facts.fact: Genoese merchants continued to reside at Pera/Galata after the Ottoman conquest under the privileges Mehmed II granted the Genoese, and a Genoese national group with its own representatives is traced there into the later seventeenth century; the end date is inferred from the terminal date of the published study and the grade reflects that inference.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf; Oxford Reference, Levant Company; https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100102153
facts.fact: English consulate and factory at Aleppo, with consuls from 1582-1584 and a continuous succession afterwards; it was the company's central Levant factory, kept a consul to 1825, and its treasury was abolished in 1783.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf
facts.fact: Levant Company factory at Smyrna with John Markham appointed consul in 1611; the factory grew from 49 members in 1661 to become the company's chief Levant station and closed with the company in 1825.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf
facts.fact: English consular post at Cairo, first granted in 1583 to Harvey Millers as consul in Cairo, Alexandria and adjacent parts; it was held with interruptions, since the company several times declined to appoint, and was revived under Crown consuls-general from 1786 until the company's end.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf
facts.fact: English consular post at Alexandria, named in the same 1583 grant and held at intervals thereafter, with a company agent resident from 1803 and a consul from 1814 until the company was dissolved.

facts.source: D. Wilson, 'List of British Consular Officials in the Ottoman Empire' (2011), sections Smyrna, Aleppo, Cairo, Alexandria, Tripoli; https://www.levantineheritage.com/pdf/List_of_British_Consular_Officials_Turkey(1581-1860)-D_Wilson.pdf
facts.fact: English consul for Tripoli in Syria, first appointed in 1583 with jurisdiction over Aleppo, Damascus, Aman, Tripoli and Jerusalem; consuls are recorded at Tripoli into the early nineteenth century, and the post ended with the company.

facts.source: Nationaal Archief, archief 1.03.01 (Directie van den Levantschen handel), contextual history: Haga mission 1610-1612, capitulation 1 July 1612, Pauw consul at Aleppo; https://www.nationaalarchief.nl/onderzoeken/archief/1.03.01/beschrijving/context
facts.fact: Dutch resident embassy and consular establishment at Constantinople created by the capitulation of 1 July 1612, which granted the ambassador and his consuls jurisdiction over Dutchmen throughout the empire; Cornelis Haga stayed until 1639 and consuls served under the Levant Directorate, whose four chambers at Amsterdam, Hoorn, Rotterdam and Middelburg sat from 1625 and whose archive runs to 1826, after which the consulates continued as state posts.

facts.source: Nationaal Archief, archief 1.03.01 (Directie van den Levantschen handel), contextual history: Haga mission 1610-1612, capitulation 1 July 1612, Pauw consul at Aleppo; https://www.nationaalarchief.nl/onderzoeken/archief/1.03.01/beschrijving/context
facts.fact: Dutch consulate at Aleppo, requested by merchants who had traded there for ten to twelve years and appointed in December 1612, with Cornelis Pauw taking up the post in 1613; the consulate was later several times entrusted to French or English consuls for lack of income and was kept by consuls after the Directorate closed in 1826.

facts.source: Nationaal Archief, archief 1.03.01 (Directie van den Levantschen handel), contextual history: Haga mission 1610-1612, capitulation 1 July 1612, Pauw consul at Aleppo; https://www.nationaalarchief.nl/onderzoeken/archief/1.03.01/beschrijving/context
facts.fact: Dutch consulate at Smyrna established by Haga after the 1612 capitulation, first held by a Venetian and then a Greek consul and from 1657 by Dutch appointees; Smyrna became the chief Dutch station in the Levant under four consuls of the De Hochepied family, 1688-1824.

facts.source: Ambassade de France en Egypte, 'Histoire du consulat de France a Alexandrie'; https://eg.ambafrance.org/Histoire-du-consulat-de-France-a; L. Tsiptsios, 'Les consuls francais au Levant: la mise en place du reseau consulaire', Les cles du Moyen-Orient; https://www.lesclesdumoyenorient.com/Les-consuls-francais-au-Levant-la-mise-en-place-du-reseau-consulaire-au-XVIIe.html; Viorel Panaite interview, Levantine Heritage Foundation; https://www.levantineheritage.com/viorel-panaite-interview.html
facts.fact: French consulate and nation at Alexandria, with a consul named from 1492 and royal appointment consolidated by the capitulations of 1535/1536 that let the king appoint consuls in Ottoman cities; the community was arrested and its property seized when the Ottoman Empire went to war with France in 1798.

facts.source: FranceArchives, 'Alexandrie (consulat general)', history of the Egyptian consulate (move to Cairo c. 1610-1620); https://francearchives.gouv.fr/findingaid/0511accf114a04452db3d87e823d2e451ba24861
facts.fact: French consulate for Egypt moved from Alexandria to Cairo around 1610-1620, when Cairo was the country's main commercial centre, leaving vice-consulates at Alexandria, Rosetta and Damietta; it ended with the 1798 rupture.

facts.source: Treaty between France and the Ottoman Empire, Paris, 25 June 1802 (capitulations renewed in all particulars); https://www.napoleon-series.org/research/government/diplomatic/c_ottoman.html; L. Tsiptsios, 'Les consuls francais au Levant: la mise en place du reseau consulaire', Les cles du Moyen-Orient; https://www.lesclesdumoyenorient.com/Les-consuls-francais-au-Levant-la-mise-en-place-du-reseau-consulaire-au-XVIIe.html
facts.fact: French consulate at Alexandria restored after the Treaty of Paris of 25 June 1802 renewed the capitulations in all their particulars and the consular system was reorganised in 1803.

facts.source: El-Mudarris and Salmon, 'Le Consulat de France a Alep au XVIIe siecle', summary of the founding date (1560 or 1562); https://www.aleppoart.com/Consulat_Alep_Gedoyn_Piquet_Arvieux.html ; L. Tsiptsios, 'Les consuls francais au Levant: la mise en place du reseau consulaire', Les cles du Moyen-Orient; https://www.lesclesdumoyenorient.com/Les-consuls-francais-au-Levant-la-mise-en-place-du-reseau-consulaire-au-XVIIe.html
facts.fact: French consulate at Aleppo, founded in 1560 or 1562 after the first royal consul for Syria was named at Tripoli in 1548; French consuls there also held the Dutch consulate from the early 1660s, and the post continued through the nineteenth century.

facts.source: A. Boppe, 'Les consulats du Levant', vol. I: Smyrne 1610-1900 (Nancy 1902), as recorded in the archives' bibliography; https://www.crlv.org/conference/smyrne-la-france-et-malte-au-xviiie-si%C3%A8cle
facts.fact: French consulate at Smyrna, founded in 1610 and continuously staffed; the consul headed the French nation and judged its members under the 1681 marine ordinance.

facts.source: Archives diplomatiques, 'Consulat de France a Seyde' (created provisionally 1611, permanently 1616; general consulate 1781; moved to Acre 1786; vice-consulate to 1821); https://archivesdiplomatiques.diplomatie.gouv.fr/ark:/14366/cb2q1jh60g7w
facts.fact: French consulate at Sidon (Seyde), created permanently in 1616 after a provisional post from 1611, previously dependent on the consulate at Tripoli; it operated without a break until 1786 and was raised to a general consulate for Syria and Palestine in 1781.

facts.source: Archives diplomatiques, 'Consulat de France a Seyde' (created provisionally 1611, permanently 1616; general consulate 1781; moved to Acre 1786; vice-consulate to 1821); https://archivesdiplomatiques.diplomatie.gouv.fr/ark:/14366/cb2q1jh60g7w
facts.fact: French consular post moved from Sidon to Acre in 1786 because of unrest, surviving there on and off as a vice-consulate until 1821.

facts.source: L. Tsiptsios, 'Les consuls francais au Levant: la mise en place du reseau consulaire', Les cles du Moyen-Orient; https://www.lesclesdumoyenorient.com/Les-consuls-francais-au-Levant-la-mise-en-place-du-reseau-consulaire-au-XVIIe.html
facts.fact: French consulate at Tripoli in Syria, the first French consular post in the Levant, founded in 1536 and formally conferred on a royal consul in 1548; it remained an echelle with a French consul after the Syrian consulate moved to Aleppo.

facts.source: L. Tsiptsios, 'Les consuls francais au Levant: la mise en place du reseau consulaire', Les cles du Moyen-Orient; https://www.lesclesdumoyenorient.com/Les-consuls-francais-au-Levant-la-mise-en-place-du-reseau-consulaire-au-XVIIe.html
facts.fact: French nation and consulate at Tunis, with its fondouk and consul heading a protected community from 1577; the consulate negotiated directly with the regency and lasted into the 1830s.

facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hanseatic League: The league in its final form' (kontore at London, Brugge, Bergen, Novgorod; Elizabeth I closes the Steelyard 1598; St Peter's court ceases 1494); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hanseatic-League/The-league-in-its-final-form; 'The Hanseatic League', WarHistory.org (Bruges kontor de facto in Antwerp from c. 1460; Antwerp kontor built from 1563, closed 1593); https://warhistory.org/article/the-hanseatic-league
facts.fact: Hanseatic kontor at Bruges, the League's western office with its own law and exemption from local jurisdiction; as the Zwin silted and the Brabant fairs drew the trade, the merchants operated de facto from Antwerp, and the office was formally wound up in the mid-sixteenth century.

facts.source: 'The Hanseatic League', WarHistory.org (Bruges kontor de facto in Antwerp from c. 1460; Antwerp kontor built from 1563, closed 1593); https://warhistory.org/article/the-hanseatic-league
facts.fact: Hanseatic kontor at Antwerp, successor to Bruges, housed from about 1560 in the Oostershuis; the city refused the League special privileges and the office closed in 1593.

facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hanseatic League: The league in its final form' (kontore at London, Brugge, Bergen, Novgorod; Elizabeth I closes the Steelyard 1598; St Peter's court ceases 1494); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hanseatic-League/The-league-in-its-final-form
facts.fact: Hanseatic kontor at the Steelyard in London, a walled community under German law and the League's diet; Elizabeth I closed it and revoked the privileges in 1598.

facts.source: Hanseatic League of today, city portrait Bergen (German Office from 1360) and UNESCO-linked account of the closure in 1754; https://www.hanse.org/en/hanse/bergen
facts.fact: Hanseatic kontor on Bryggen at Bergen, founded about 1360 and the longest-lived of the four offices, with its own district and courts; it closed in 1754 and was replaced by an office of Norwegian citizens.

facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hanseatic League: The league in its final form' (kontore at London, Brugge, Bergen, Novgorod; Elizabeth I closes the Steelyard 1598; St Peter's court ceases 1494); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hanseatic-League/The-league-in-its-final-form
facts.fact: Hanseatic kontor of St Peter at Novgorod, a self-governing enclosure with its own statute; Ivan III expelled the merchants in 1478 and the office formally ceased to be a kontor in 1494.

facts.source: Kaunas city municipality, city history (Hanseatic office 1441-1532); https://en.kaunas.lt/city/city-history; Hanseatic League of today, city portrait Kaunas (kontor 1441-1532); https://www.hanse.org/en/hanse/kaunas
facts.fact: Hanseatic office at Kaunas (Kovno) in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, opened in 1441 as the League's only Lithuanian kontor and closed in 1532.

facts.source: e-architect, 'Fondaco dei Tedeschi: OMA Venice Architecture' (German merchants' hostel and warehouse from the 13th century, customs house under Napoleon 1806); https://www.e-architect.com/venice/fondaco-dei-tedeschi
facts.fact: Fondaco dei Tedeschi at the Rialto, the compulsory hostel and warehouse for German merchants in Venice from the thirteenth century, mostly men from Nuremberg and Augsburg; it functioned until the Republic fell in 1797 and became a customs house under Napoleon.

facts.source: Columbia University, Media Center for Art History, 'Fondaco dei Turchi' (assigned to Ottoman merchants 1621, occupied until 1838); https://mcid.mcah.columbia.edu/work/w0000340 ; Venice and its lagoons, 'Fondaco dei Turchi'; https://www.venicethefuture.com/schede/uk/125-aliusid=125.htm
facts.fact: Fondaco dei Turchi on the Grand Canal, assigned by the Senate in March 1621 as the residence and warehouse of Ottoman merchants in Venice, with controlled entry and internal rules; Ottoman traders lived there until 1838.

facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Muscovy Company' (charter 1555; privileges ended 1649); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Muscovy-Company ; Encyclopedia.com, 'Russia Company' (expulsion of 1649, Archangel excepted); https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/british-and-irish-history/russia-company
facts.fact: English Muscovy Company house and factory in Moscow, chartered in 1555 with customs exemption and control of its own settlement; Tsar Alexei revoked the exemption in 1646 and expelled the English merchants in 1649.

facts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Muscovy Company' (charter 1555; privileges ended 1649); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Muscovy-Company ; Encyclopedia.com, 'Russia Company' (expulsion of 1649, Archangel excepted); https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/british-and-irish-history/russia-company
facts.fact: English company factory at the northern port of Kholmogory/Arkhangelsk, the company's landing place for the Russian trade from 1555; the 1649 expulsion closed the privileged residence, Archangel alone being left open to English shipping.
Babur defeats the Lodi sultan at Panipat and founds the Mughal empire in Hindustan; the dynasty rules from Agra and Delhi until the British occupy Delhi.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Sher Shah Suri drives Humayun out of Hindustan and founds the Sur empire at Delhi; it collapses in civil war on his successors' defeat in 1555-56.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Delhi sultanate rules from Delhi through the Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties; the change of dynasty in 1414 and 1451 leaves the state and its seat unchanged.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Babur makes Agra his seat after Panipat; Akbar moves the court to the new palace city of Fatehpur Sikri beside Agra c.1571, which has no separate map location, and abandons it for the north in 1585.
facts.source: Vincent A. Smith, Akbar the Great Mogul, 1542-1605 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1917): Fathpur-Sikri begun 1569, capital established there c.1571, 'ceased to reside at Fathpur-Sikri in 1585'; letter of Akbar 'to Lahore where we reside'. https://archive.org/details/akbargreatmogul100smit

facts.fact: Akbar shifts his residence to Lahore for his north-western campaigns and stays in the north for thirteen years.
facts.source: Vincent A. Smith, Akbar the Great Mogul, 1542-1605 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1917): Fathpur-Sikri begun 1569, capital established there c.1571, 'ceased to reside at Fathpur-Sikri in 1585'; letter of Akbar 'to Lahore where we reside'. https://archive.org/details/akbargreatmogul100smit

facts.fact: Akbar returns to Agra, which remains the Mughal capital under Jahangir.
facts.source: Vincent A. Smith, Akbar the Great Mogul, 1542-1605 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1917): Fathpur-Sikri begun 1569, capital established there c.1571, 'ceased to reside at Fathpur-Sikri in 1585'; letter of Akbar 'to Lahore where we reside'. https://archive.org/details/akbargreatmogul100smit

facts.fact: Shah Jahan builds Shahjahanabad at Delhi from 1638 and makes it the Mughal capital; the court stays there, under British occupation after 1803, to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Red Fort Complex (list 231): built as the palace fort of Shahjahanabad, 'the new capital' of Shah Jahan, begun 1638/39. https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/231

facts.fact: Babur's victory at Panipat puts the Delhi doab under Mughal rule.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Sher Shah's victory at Chausa and Kannauj drives the Mughals from the doab; the Sur empire holds Agra and Delhi.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Humayun recovers Delhi and Agra from the Sur successors; the Mughals hold the doab until the British occupy Delhi.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Lake's victory at Laswari and the treaty with Sindhia give the East India Company the Delhi doab; the Mughal emperor remains a pensioner in the Red Fort.
facts.source: Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. I-II (Calcutta, 1932-34): Nadir Shah 1739, Ahmad Shah Durrani's invasions to 1761, British occupation of Delhi 1803. https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.511649

facts.fact: The Mughals take the Punjab plains from the Lodi sultanate; Lahore becomes an imperial residence and second city.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals; full text at Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Ahmad Shah Durrani's repeated invasions end Mughal authority in the Punjab; he appoints governors at Lahore and Multan.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: The Sikh misl confederacy takes Lahore and the central Punjab plains from the Afghans after 1764; no single ruler holds them until Ranjit Singh.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: Ranjit Singh takes Lahore in 1799 and brings the central Punjab plains under the Sikh state.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: The Durrani empire holds Peshawar and the Khyber approaches; Peshawar is its winter capital.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: Ranjit Singh takes Attock in 1813 and installs governors at Peshawar after 1818, holding the province to the end of the timeline.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: The Durrani empire extends over the Pashtun hill country west of the Indus (Bannu, Tank, Zhob, Dera Ghazi Khan).
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs 'become masters of Lahore' 1764; by 1793 masters of the Upper Punjab as far as Attock; Ranjit Singh's 'acquisition of Lahore in 1799'; Multan captured 1818; Peshawar made over 1818-34. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: The Mughals hold the Haryana plains south-west of Delhi (Hisar, Hansi) after the Lodi collapse; Mughal authority there dissolves in the 1760s.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs masters of Hariana by 1768-78; British occupation of Delhi 1803. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: The Company's victories in the Second Anglo-Maratha War bring the Haryana plains under British administration.
facts.source: J. D. Cunningham, A History of the Sikhs (London, 1849/1853): Sikhs masters of Hariana by 1768-78; British occupation of Delhi 1803. https://archive.org/details/cunninghamshisto00cunnuoft

facts.fact: Ala al-Din Hasan Bahman Shah throws off Delhi's authority in the Deccan and founds the Bahmani sultanate with its capital at Gulbarga.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Yusuf Adil Khan makes himself independent at Bijapur as the Bahmani sultanate breaks up; the Adil Shahi sultanate lasts until Aurangzeb's conquest.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah founds the Nizam Shahi sultanate at Ahmadnagar out of the Bahmani province of Daulatabad.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk establishes the Imad Shahi sultanate of Berar at Ellichpur; Ahmadnagar annexes it in 1574.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Qasim Barid secures the Bahmani capital at Bidar, where his Barid Shahi successors rule the shrunken sultanate until Bijapur annexes it.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk makes himself independent at Golconda; the Qutb Shahi state ends with Aurangzeb's siege of Golconda.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Dilawar Khan and his son Hoshang Shah make Malwa an independent sultanate with its capital at Mandu; Akbar annexes it in 1561.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Faruqi rulers establish themselves at Burhanpur in Khandesh; Akbar's officers take Asirgarh and annex the state in 1601.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigarh, converting his Maratha following into a sovereign kingdom; the Maratha power ends with the British conquest of 1818.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 1 (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32141

facts.fact: With Vijayanagara's collapse the Wodeyars rule Mysore as an independent kingdom; Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan hold it until the British storm Seringapatam.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Nizam-ul-Mulk defeats the imperial governor at Shakarkhelda in 1724, becomes independent and fixes his residence at Hyderabad.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: The Nayak governors of Madurai under Vijayanagara become hereditary rulers; their line ends when the nawab of Arcot takes Madurai in 1736.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: Sevappa Nayak establishes the Nayak ruling house of Thanjavur; in 1674 the Maratha general Venkaji (Ekoji) supplants it.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: Venkaji, half-brother of Shivaji, takes the Thanjavur throne; his Maratha successors rule until the British take over the state in 1799.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The Mughal governor of the Carnatic, Sadatullah Khan, establishes the nawabi of Arcot, which dominates the Tamil country until the British annexation of 1801.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: The Keladi (Ikkeri) Nayaks rule the Kanara hill country from Ikkeri and later Bednur until Haidar Ali annexes their realm.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Vijayanagara absorbs the Hoysala kingdom, whose lands pass to Harihara and Bukka's new state.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Bahmani sultanate takes the Kalyana and Bijapur districts of the Deccan from Delhi.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Barid Shahi rulers hold Bidar and its immediate districts as their sultanate.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Bijapur controls the western half of the Kalyana country, including the city of Bijapur.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur annexes the Bidar sultanate.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Vijayanagara holds the Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: After the defeat at Talikota, Bijapur takes the Raichur doab and the Tungabhadra country from Vijayanagara.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Wodeyar rulers of Mysore become independent as Vijayanagara's power breaks up after Talikota.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Keladi Nayakas rule the Karnataka hill country from Ikkeri as an independent house after Vijayanagara's collapse.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: After the storming of Seringapatam the British take direct control of Mysore.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: Aurangzeb's conquest of Bijapur brings the Bijapur districts of the Deccan under direct Mughal rule.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Nizam's Hyderabad state holds the Bijapur and Raichur districts after the Mughal collapse in the Deccan.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: The Bahmani sultanate extends its rule over the Marathwada and Desh districts of the western Deccan.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Ahmadnagar holds the northern Maratha country and the Marathwada districts around Daulatabad.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Bijapur holds the southern Desh and the Malnad districts of the western Deccan.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Shah Jahan extinguishes the Ahmadnagar sultanate and the Marathwada districts pass under Mughal administration.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Shivaji's Maratha kingdom holds the Desh districts around Pune and Raigarh.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 1 (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32141

facts.fact: The Marathas take the Belgaum and Malnad districts from Bijapur's successors.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 1 (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32141

facts.fact: The British defeat the Peshwa and annex his Deccan territory.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 3: Sunset over Maharashtra (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207755

facts.fact: The Nizam retains the Marathwada districts around Aurangabad and Nander.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: The Bahmani sultanate holds the Konkan coast from Chaul northwards.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Ahmadnagar sultanate holds the northern Konkan and the coastal districts south of it.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Mughal power reaches the Konkan coast with the extinction of Ahmadnagar.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Marathas hold the Konkan coast north of Goa, apart from the Portuguese ports.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 1 (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32141

facts.fact: The British annex the southern Konkan after the defeat of the Peshwa.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 3: Sunset over Maharashtra (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207755

facts.fact: The Portuguese acquire Bassein and its territory from Gujarat by treaty.
facts.source: Frederick Charles Danvers, The Portuguese in India, vol. 2 (London: Allen, 1894); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/portugueseinindi02danv

facts.fact: The Marathas take Bassein from the Portuguese.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Bombay Presidency, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207009

facts.fact: Bombay passes to the Portuguese with the rest of the Bassein territory.
facts.source: Frederick Charles Danvers, The Portuguese in India, vol. 2 (London: Allen, 1894); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/portugueseinindi02danv

facts.fact: Bombay comes to the English crown as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry and is leased to the East India Company.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Bombay Presidency, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207009

facts.fact: The Portuguese hold the fortified port of Chaul.
facts.source: Frederick Charles Danvers, The Portuguese in India, vol. 2 (London: Allen, 1894); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/portugueseinindi02danv

facts.fact: The Marathas take Chaul from the Portuguese.
facts.source: G. S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, vol. 1 (Bombay: Phoenix, 1946); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32141

facts.fact: The Bahmani sultans keep their capital district at Bidar after the loss of the rest of Kalyana.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Muhammad Shah I of the Bahmanis seizes Golconda and Kaulas from Warangal.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Ahmad Shah Wali defeats and kills the ruler of Warangal and annexes most of his territory.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Qutb Shahi sultans rule the Telangana country from Golconda.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Aurangzeb's siege and capture of Golconda brings the Telangana country under Mughal rule.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Nizam's Hyderabad state holds the Telangana districts around Golconda and Warangal.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: The Qutb Shahi court professes Twelver Shi'ism as the state confession.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Vijayanagara rules the Rayalaseema districts and the Tungabhadra marches south of the Krishna.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Deva Raya I annexes the Reddi kingdom of Kondavidu after its internal confusion.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Krishna Deva Raya's campaigns carry Vijayanagara's frontier to the Krishna and take the coastal districts of Kalinga.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Golconda takes the Andhra coast from the collapsing Vijayanagara and Orissa frontier.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: Bijapur destroys the Aravidu remnant of Vijayanagara and occupies the Rayalaseema country.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: Mughal conquest of Bijapur and Golconda brings the Andhra country under the empire.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Nizam rules the Andhra districts from Hyderabad.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Hyderabad State (Calcutta, 1909); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207369

facts.fact: The Company receives the Northern Circars from the Nizam and later the ceded districts of the Deccan.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: Vijayanagara wipes out the sultanate of Madurai and rules the Tamil country up to Rameswaram.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: The Nayak governors of Madurai hold the Pandya country as hereditary rulers.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The Nayaks of Thanjavur rule the Kaveri delta.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: Venkaji and his Maratha successors take and hold the Thanjavur kingdom.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The nawabs of Arcot rule the northern Tamil districts from Arcot and Vellore.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: Mysore extends its rule over the Kongu country and the Baramahal.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: British conquest and cession bring the Tamil districts under Company rule.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: The Portuguese hold the Coromandel port of Negapatam.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The Dutch take Negapatam and Nagore from the Portuguese and hold them as their Coromandel headquarters.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The British annex the Dutch settlements of Negapatam and Nagore.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The Danish East India Company obtains Tranquebar from the nayak of Tanjore and holds it under annual tribute.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: The British take Tranquebar during the Napoleonic wars and restore it to Denmark in 1814.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: Tranquebar returns to Danish rule after the peace.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 2 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146794

facts.fact: Fort St George at Madraspatnam becomes the Company's fortified headquarters on the Coromandel coast.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: The French establish their principal Indian settlement at Pondicherry.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: Pondicherry is occupied by the British through the Napoleonic wars.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: Pondicherry is restored to France and remains the seat of French India.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793
