facts.fact: Ahmad Shah Wali moves the Bahmani capital from Gulbarga to Bidar after annexing Warangal.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Delhi: Orient Longman, 2007), ch. 9-16; full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303

facts.fact: After the disaster at Talikota the Vijayanagara court withdraws from the capital to Penukonda.
facts.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Madras, vol. 1 (Calcutta, 1908); full text at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146793

facts.fact: The Bengal Sultanate holds the old Lakhnauti heartland in northern and western Bengal (Gaur, Devkot, Bogra).
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 263: Iliyas master of Western Bengal in 1345, his capital Pandua.)

facts.fact: The Bengal Sultanate absorbs the western delta and the Hooghly towns of Satgaon, Nadia and Khulna.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 263: in 1352 Iliyas 'established his dominion over the whole of Bengal'; Satgaon and Pandua as royal seats.)

facts.fact: The Bengal Sultanate takes eastern Bengal around Sonargaon, Mymensingh and Khalifatabad; one account dates the fall of Sonargaon to 1352 and another to 1362.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 263: 'he did not obtain possession of Sonargaon until 1362, when Ghazi Shah was expelled'; the chronology gives the overthrow of Ghazi Shah under 1352.)

facts.fact: The Bengal court moves from Pandua back to Gaur, which the sultans rebuild as their capital.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 268: Mahmud Shah 'rebuilt the old capital, Gaur'; Husain Shah later shifts the court to Ikdala and his successor restores Gaur.)

facts.fact: Sher Khan Sur takes Gaur in 1538 and, after defeating Humayun at Chausa, rules Bengal as a province of the Sur empire.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. xi, pp. 274-276: Gaur sacked 6 April 1538, Sher Khan assumes the royal title, Bengal divided into prefectures after 1540.)

facts.fact: With the collapse of the Sur empire the Afghan governors of Bengal rule as independent sultans, first at Gaur and later from Tanda; the line ends with Daud Khan Karrani.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (pp. 110-111: Sulaiman Karrani 'established his independence in Bengal when the power of the Sur dynasty declined', died 1572; Daud Khan defeated 1576.)

facts.fact: The Afghan sultans of Bengal hold the whole Bengal plain until Daud Khan Karrani is defeated and killed near Rajmahal in July 1576.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International, 2007), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara-Bahmanids and Mughal expansion. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303 (pp. 152-153: 1574 Bihar, Tukarao 3 March 1575, Daud killed near Rajmahal July 1576, 'Bengal was now finally annexed').

facts.fact: The Mughals annex western and central Bengal after the battle of Rajmahal and govern it as the subah of Bengal, with the seat later moving from Rajmahal to Dacca and then to Murshidabad.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International, 2007), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara-Bahmanids and Mughal expansion. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303 (pp. 152-153, annexation 1576); Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Bengal, vol. i (Calcutta, 1909), 'History' and the Murshidabad district article (Murshid Quli Khan moves the seat of government from Dacca to Maksudabad). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146786 (Murshid Quli Khan moves the seat of government from Dacca to Maksudabad, thereafter Murshidabad).

facts.fact: After the fall of the Karranis the Bhati country of eastern Bengal is held by the Baro-Bhuyan confederacy of landholders under Isa Khan and his son Musa Khan.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International, 2007), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara-Bahmanids and Mughal expansion. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303 (p. 153: 'Isa Khan in East Bengal' continued to resist after 1576); The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 161: Islam Khan governor with a mission to subdue the Afghans, 'Usman Khan defeated and killed 1612).

facts.fact: The Baro-Bhuyan chiefs hold eastern Bengal from Sonargaon to Khalifatabad against the Mughals.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International, 2007), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara-Bahmanids and Mughal expansion. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303 (p. 153); The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 161, campaign of Islam Khan to 1612).

facts.fact: The Mughals complete the conquest of eastern Bengal with the submission of Musa Khan and the defeat of the Afghan chiefs, and govern it from Dacca.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 161: Islam Khan's campaign, defeat of 'Usman Khan 1612); Imperial Gazetteer of India, Provincial Series: Bengal, vol. i (Calcutta, 1909), 'History' and the Murshidabad district article (Murshid Quli Khan moves the seat of government from Dacca to Maksudabad). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.146786 (seat of government at Dacca until Murshid Quli Khan).

facts.fact: The Mughal emperor confers the diwani of Bengal on the English East India Company on 16 August 1765, and the Company rules the Bengal plain.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxv, p. 409: 'on 16 August, 1765, the emperor Shah Alam... conferred that office on the British East India Company').

facts.fact: Malik Sarwar, governor of Kara-Manikpur, establishes himself independently at Jaunpur; his successors, the Sharqi sultans, rule Awadh and the Ganges valley until Buhlul Lodi recovers the city.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. x and dynastic chronology: 'Malik Sarvar, Khvaja Jahan 1394', Sharqi kings to Husain Shah 1458-1479, 'Recovery of Jaunpur' under Buhlul Lodi).

facts.fact: The Sharqi sultans hold Awadh, with their capital at Jaunpur.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. x; p. 251 'Malik Sarvar establishes his independence in Jaunpur').

facts.fact: The Sharqi sultans extend their rule over the middle Ganges valley around Varanasi, Azamgarh and Gorakhpur.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. x, pp. 255-258: Husain Sharqi's invasion of Delhi and his flight to Bihar through this country; 'Husain flees to Bengal').

facts.fact: Buhlul Lodi recovers Jaunpur and Awadh for the Delhi Sultanate.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. ix, pp. 233-234 'Recovery of Jaunpur'; ch. x chronology, Husain Shah 1458-1479).

facts.fact: The Delhi Sultanate holds the middle Ganges valley after the fall of Jaunpur, and Sikandar Lodi campaigns there.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. ix, pp. 237-238: Sikandar's campaigns round Jaunpur, Chunar and Arail, 1494).

facts.fact: Babur's victory at Panipat brings Awadh into the Mughal empire.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. ix, p. 250: 'Defeat and death of Ibrahim at Panipat').

facts.fact: The Mughals take the middle Ganges valley with the fall of the Lodi sultanate.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (chs. on Babur and Humayun); The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 250).

facts.fact: Sher Shah's victory at Chausa and his occupation of Delhi give the Sur empire Awadh.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (ch. xi, p. 275: Chausa and the Sur assumption of the imperial throne, 1540).

facts.fact: The Sur empire holds the middle Ganges valley, where Sher Shah builds his administrative works.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 275); Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International, 2007), chs. on the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara-Bahmanids and Mughal expansion. https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303 (pp. 152-153).

facts.fact: Awadh returns to the Mughal empire after the collapse of the Sur dynasty and remains an imperial province until Saadat Khan.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 432: 'Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk was appointed governor of Awadh on 9th September, 1722... succeeded in converting that province into an independent state').

facts.fact: The Mughals hold the middle Ganges valley around Varanasi, Azamgarh and Gorakhpur as part of the subah of Awadh.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (chs. on Akbar and Aurangzib); Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 432).

facts.fact: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk, appointed governor of Awadh in 1722, makes the province a hereditary state with its court at Awadh and later at Lucknow.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 432); The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi: Lucknow as the nawab's capital, Asaf-ud-daula, 1784).

facts.fact: The nawabs of Awadh hold the Awadh country as an effectively independent state.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 432, 'converting that province into an independent state').

facts.fact: Asaf-ud-daula moves the Awadh court from Faizabad-Awadh to Lucknow, which becomes the capital.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi, p. 349: Lucknow under Asaf-ud-daula, the Imambarah built 1784).

facts.fact: The nawabs of Awadh hold the eastern districts around Azamgarh and Gorakhpur.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi, pp. 353-354: the territory ceded by the treaty of November 1801 'formed a barrier between the dominions of the Wazir and any foreign enemy').

facts.fact: The rajas of Benares hold the Varanasi country as a zamindari under the nawabs of Awadh.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi and the index: Benares and the nawab of Oudh); Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 432).

facts.fact: The East India Company acquires the sovereignty and revenue of the Benares country from the nawab of Awadh; the raja continues to hold it as a zamindar under the Company.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi: Benares and the treaty arrangements with Oudh, 1775-1781).

facts.fact: By the treaty of November 1801 the nawab of Awadh cedes his eastern districts, including Gorakhpur and Azamgarh, to the East India Company.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi, pp. 353-354: 'The date of the treaty was November, 1801. The required territory was ceded.').

facts.fact: The Mughals hold Katehr, the country later called Rohilkhand, from the fall of the Lodi dynasty.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (chs. on Babur); Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 434: 'The province of Katehr passed into the hands of an adventurer named Ali Muhammad Khan Ruhela, and became known as Ruhelkhand').

facts.fact: The Sur empire holds Katehr between the Ganges and the hills.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. III: Turks and Afghans, ed. Wolseley Haig (Cambridge UP, 1928), ch. x 'The Kingdom of Jaunpur', ch. xi 'The Kingdom of Bengal' (Iliyas Shah, Pandua, Sher Shah, Chausa), and the dynastic chronology. https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory03raps (p. 275, Sur conquest of Delhi 1540).

facts.fact: Katehr returns to the Mughal empire after the Sur collapse and remains an imperial district until the Rohilla Afghans take it.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 434: Muhammad Shah's expedition against the Rohilla stronghold of Bangarh near Budaun); The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 370: 'Rise of the Rohilla power').

facts.fact: Ali Muhammad Khan Ruhela, an Afghan adventurer, makes himself master of Katehr and founds the Rohilla state of Rohilkhand with its centre at Bareilly.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 434: Katehr passes to Ali Muhammad Khan Ruhela and becomes Ruhelkhand; his defeat and release, reoccupation of Ruhelkhand); The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxii, p. 217: Rohilkhand 'governed by a loose confederacy of chiefs').

facts.fact: The Rohilla Afghans hold Katehr, which takes the name Rohilkhand.
facts.source: Ashribadi Lal Srivastava, The Mughul Empire 1526-1803 A.D., 5th ed. (Agra, 1966), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal and on the later Mughuls (Saadat Khan governor of Awadh, 9 September 1722; Alivardi Khan, 1740). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.112611 (p. 434); The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937), chs. on Akbar's conquest of Bengal (1574-76), Jahangir's Bengal, Aurangzib's subahs, and the chronology of the decline (Murshid Quli Khan; Orissa surrendered to the Marathas, 1751). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 370).

facts.fact: The Rohilla war of 1774 gives Rohilkhand to the nawab of Awadh, whose troops with a British brigade conquer it; the Afghans recover parts of it in the 1790s but the country is ceded to the Company in 1801.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxii, pp. 217-219: the Rohilla war, secret agreement of 1773, expedition of 1774; ch. xxi, p. 348: 'the restoration of their possessions to the Afghans under Hamid Ali Khan').

facts.fact: Rohilkhand is among the territories ceded to the East India Company by the nawab of Awadh in November 1801.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. V: British India 1497-1858, ed. H. H. Dodwell (Cambridge UP, 1929), ch. vii 'Clive in Bengal' (Diwani, 16 August 1765), ch. xxi 'Oudh and the Carnatic' (Rohilla war, cession of 1801), ch. xxii (Treaty of Deogaon, 15 December 1803; Calcutta founded 1690). https://archive.org/details/cambridgehistory05raps (ch. xxi, pp. 353-354, treaty of November 1801).

facts.fact: Sulaiman Karrani's Afghans conquer northern Orissa as far as Jajpur and Cuttack, and hold it after the fall of the Bengal sultanate until Man Singh's campaign.
facts.source: R. D. Banerji, History of Orissa from the Earliest Times to the British Period, vol. i (Prabasi Press, 1930), ch. xxii 'The Last of the Gajapatis' (Mukunda Harichandana, Karrani conquest 1568, Man Singh 1592). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.281018 (ch. xxii, pp. 341-346: 'in 1568... the kingdom fell'; 'For 24 years, from 1568 till 1592, there was anarchy in Orissa and very little is known of the short Afghan rule').

facts.fact: The Qutb Shahi sultans of Golconda oust the Gajapati rulers of southern Orissa and rule Ganjam through a faujdar at Chicacole.
facts.source: R. D. Banerji, History of Orissa from the Earliest Times to the British Period, vol. i (Prabasi Press, 1930), ch. xxii. https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.281018 (ch. xxii, pp. 348-350: the southern Gajapatis 'ruling as subordinates of the Qutb-Shahi Sultans of Golconda'; 'Chicacole became the seat of a Qutb Shahi faujdar some time before 1641').

facts.fact: Man Singh defeats the Orissa rebels at Midnapore in April 1592, occupies Cuttack, and Orissa is annexed to the Mughal empire.
facts.source: The Cambridge History of India, vol. IV: The Mughul Period, ed. R. Burn (Cambridge UP, 1937). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.276999 (p. 107: 'Man Singh... defeated the rebel forces at Mednipur on 18 April, 1592... Orissa was at length completely subdued'); R. D. Banerji, History of Orissa from the Earliest Times to the British Period, vol. i (Prabasi Press, 1930), ch. xxii. https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.281018 (pp. 350-351).

facts.fact: Daendels abolishes the Banten sultanate in 1808-13 and the territory passes to direct Dutch rule.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: In the agreements of 1677 Amangkurat II recognised Batavia's boundaries as reaching the Indian Ocean, so that the Priangan highlands became VOC territory.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Sunda kingdom holds the Cirebon district on the north coast.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Sunan Gunungjati settles at Cirebon after 1552 and founds a separate royal line there.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Cirebon rules the north coast of west Java as an independent sultanate.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Cirebon's princes are taken under VOC protection in 1680-1; the territory is later administered directly.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Samudera-Pasai holds the ports of Pedir and Pasai on the north Sumatran coast.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Aceh takes Pedir and Pasai in 1524, expelling their Portuguese garrison.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Aru-based polity of east Sumatra holds Deli.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Iskandar Muda of Aceh conquers Deli in 1612, extending Aceh's rule down the east coast.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Aru-based polity holds the Rokan and Kampar river districts.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Aceh takes Aru in 1613, adding its mainland districts on the east Sumatran coast.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Aceh rules the Siak river district after the conquest of Aru.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: A Siak sultanate establishes itself on the Sumatran east coast in the early eighteenth century, independent of Aceh.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Siak rules the lower Siak river and its ports.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Banten extends its authority over the districts of Lampung in south Sumatra.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: With Banten's abolition Lampung passes under direct Dutch rule.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: A Dutch expedition takes Palembang in 1821; in 1823 the sultanate is placed under direct Dutch rule.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The English East India Company establishes itself at Bencoolen on the west coast of Sumatra.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: Under the Anglo-Dutch treaty of London (1824) Bencoolen is handed to the Dutch.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Dutch columns defeat the Padri movement and impose direct rule in Minangkabau (Padri war, 1821-38).
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Brunei's court adopts Islam with the first sultan in the later fourteenth century.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: A Malay sultanate is founded at Pontianak on the west coast of Borneo in 1771.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Pontianak rules its river mouth and immediate hinterland.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The king of Gowa adopts Islam in 1605 and it is imposed on the Bugis-Makassarese area by 1611.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: After the treaty of Bungaya (1667) and a second campaign the VOC takes the Makassarese fort of Ujung Pandang (Fort Rotterdam).
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The VOC builds a fortress at Menado in 1658 against Spanish and Ternaten influence.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: After 1677 the VOC establishes itself in Gorontalo and the small Minahasan states.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Portuguese build a fortress on Ternate in 1522 and hold it until the Ternatens expel them in 1575.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: A Spanish fleet from the Philippines occupies Tidore in 1606 and holds it, as the ally of Tidore against Portuguese Ternate, until the Spanish withdraw in 1663.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The VOC recovers eastern Ternate from the Spanish in 1607 and keeps a fortress there thereafter.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: After Sultan Amsterdam's surrender in 1681 Ternate becomes a VOC-controlled state and the Company garrison holds the island.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Ternate adopts Islam under Sultan Zainal Abidin at the end of the fifteenth century.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Ambon becomes the main centre of Portuguese activity in the Moluccas.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The VOC takes Ambon from the Portuguese in 1605 and makes it the centre of its clove monopoly.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The VOC conquers Banda in 1621 and deports or kills most of its population.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The VOC occupies Kupang on Timor in 1653 as its base for the sandalwood trade.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Portuguese establish their base at Lifau in western Timor in the mid-seventeenth century, moving to Dili in 1769.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Legazpi takes Cebu in 1565 and makes it the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Spanish arms and missions extend to Panay and Negros in the first years after Cebu.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Legazpi founds the city of Manila in 1571 on the site of the Rajah's settlement and makes it the capital of the Philippines.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Spanish conquest and mission stations bring central Luzon under colonial rule.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Augustinian missions and garrisons extend Spanish rule to the Ilocos coast.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Spanish conquest reaches the Bicol peninsula in the 1570s.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: The Spanish build the fortress of Zamboanga in 1635 as a base against the sultanates of Mindanao and Sulu.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Spain reoccupies and rebuilds the fortress of Zamboanga in 1718.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland: Arthur H. Clark, 1903): 'The city of Manila was founded by the adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi'; https://archive.org/details/philippineislan03bourgoog

facts.fact: Majapahit conquers Bali in 1343 and rules it through Javanese governors until the Balinese courts regain independence as Majapahit collapses.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Amangkurat II cedes Semarang directly to the VOC in the agreements of 1677.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Banjarese court of south-east Borneo adopts Islam in the early sixteenth century.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: Gowa's campaigns of 1608-11 impose Islam on the Bugis states, including Bone.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Dominican missionaries build and hold a fortress on Solor from 1562 until the Dutch expel them in 1613.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Dutch destroy the Portuguese fortress at Solor in 1613 and dominate the Flores-Solor channel.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: The Sulu sultanate is founded in the early fifteenth century as an Islamic state.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: Sharif Kabungsuwan brings Islam to the Maguindanao valley in the early sixteenth century and founds a sultanate.
facts.source: D. G. E. Hall, A History of South-East Asia (London: Macmillan, 1955), full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/in.gov.ignca.3869

facts.fact: Ali Mughayat Syah of Aceh takes Daya on the west coast in 1520, the first of his conquests.
facts.source: M. C. Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c.1200, 4th ed. (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008), chs. 2-13, full text at Internet Archive; https://archive.org/details/m.-c.-ricklefs-a-history-of-modern-indonesia-since-c.-1200-red-globe-press-2008

facts.fact: Legazpi's Spaniards take Manila and extend Spanish rule over the Tagalog and Pampanga lowlands of Luzon.
facts.source: E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, The Philippine Islands 1493-1898, vol. 3 (Cleveland, 1903): Legazpi at Cebu 1565 and Manila 1571. https://archive.org/details/philippineisland03blai

facts.fact: The Sinhalese kingdom shifts its seat from Kurunegala to Gampola in the mid-fourteenth century; Gampola remains the royal residence into the fifteenth century.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: Alagakkonara builds the fortress of Kotte near Colombo and the Sinhalese court moves there, beginning the Kotte dynasty.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: The Sinhalese kingdom holds the south-western and southern lowlands; from the early fifteenth century its capital is Kotte.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: Mayadunne, one of the three brothers who divide Kotte in 1521, rules from Sitawaka as an independent kingdom until its absorption by Kandy in 1594.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: Sitawaka itself is the seat of Mayadunne's kingdom.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: A separate kingdom of the hill country around Senkadagalapura (Kandy) emerges in the late fifteenth century and survives Portuguese and Dutch pressure until the Kandyan Convention of 1815.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: The Kandyan kingdom holds the central highlands around Senkadagalapura.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: Kandy extends its authority over the north-central dry zone and the Vanni after the fall of Sitawaka.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.fact: Portugal deposes the Arya Chakravarti dynasty of Jaffna and holds the northern peninsula as a Portuguese province.
facts.source: W. H. Mills, A Short History of Ceylon (Macmillan, 1926), chs. V-VII, IX: Kotte founded by Alagakkonara c. 1412; Dharmapala's Donation of 1580, Portuguese proclamation 1597; Jaffna 'reduced to subjection' 1619 and held 'until its capture by the Dutch in 1658'; Dutch occupation 1656-1796. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.7980

facts.source: J. Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, abridged C. H. Payne (New York, 1914). https://archive.org/details/todsannalsofraja00todjrich

facts.fact: The Gaikwad's officers hold Broach for the Maratha confederacy until the district is made over to the Company.
facts.source: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, vol. IV: Ahmedabad (Bombay, 1879), ch. VIII Acquisition 1802-1817. https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.3354

facts.fact: Rana Kumbha of Mewar brings the eastern districts round Mandalgarh and Bhilwara under Chittor.
facts.source: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India 800-1700 (New Age International), Mewar section: Rana Kumbha (1433-68). https://archive.org/details/history-of-medieval-india-800-1700_202303; J. Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, abridged C. H. Payne (New York, 1914), Mewar annals. https://archive.org/details/todsannalsofraja00todjrich

facts.fact: The Hada Rajputs hold the Hadoti country on the Chambal, with Kota as a separate Hara house from the seventeenth century.
facts.source: J. Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, abridged C. H. Payne (New York, 1914), Mewar annals. https://archive.org/details/todsannalsofraja00todjrich

facts.fact: Shah Beg Arghun holds Kandahar after the Timurid collapse until Babur takes the city.
facts.source: H. M. Elliot and J. Dowson cited in Gazetteer of the Province of Sind (1907), ch. III History, and M. Elphinstone, An Account of the Kingdom of Caubul (1815). https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.62034

facts.fact: Daman is a Gujarati sarkar of the sultanate until the Portuguese take the port.
facts.source: E. C. Bayley, The Local Muhammadan Dynasties: Gujarat (1886), revenue list of the sarkars: 'The port of Daman, dependent on Surat'. https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.529161

facts.fact: The Shah Mir sultans make Sunni Islam the religion of the Kashmiri state.
facts.source: W. R. Lawrence, The Valley of Kashmir (London, 1895), ch. VII: Shah Mir 'became king of Kashmir, under the name of Shams-ud-din'. https://archive.org/details/valleyofkashmir00lawruoft

facts.fact: Nadir Shah's Persian army takes Kandahar, Ghazni and Sistan from the Hotak Afghans; the provinces stay under his Persian government until his death in 1747.
facts.source: W. H. Moreland and A. Yusuf Ali, eds., Imperial Gazetteer of India: Afghanistan and Nepal (1908); P. Sykes, A History of Persia, 3rd ed. (London, 1930), chs. on the Safavids and Nadir Shah. https://archive.org/details/historyofpersia02syke

facts.fact: Timurid Herat's governors hold Sistan and Farah until Babur's Arghun successors and then the Safavids take the region after 1507.
facts.source: W. H. Moreland and A. Yusuf Ali, eds., Imperial Gazetteer of India: Afghanistan and Nepal (1908); P. Sykes, A History of Persia, 3rd ed. (London, 1930), chs. on the Safavids and Nadir Shah. https://archive.org/details/historyofpersia02syke

facts.fact: Babur's conquest of Hindustan leaves Kandahar with the Mughal empire; it is held by imperial governors until the Safavids take it in 1556.
facts.source: W. H. Moreland and A. Yusuf Ali, eds., Imperial Gazetteer of India: Afghanistan and Nepal (1908); P. Sykes, A History of Persia, 3rd ed. (London, 1930), chs. on the Safavids and Nadir Shah. https://archive.org/details/historyofpersia02syke
